Mr. Speaker, on Friday night just before the house adjourned I referred to a paper written by some of the departmental heads in Ottawa in 1932. I was speaking from memory and I made a mistake of two years because the paper was written by Dr. Hugh Spence and R. K. Carnochan in 1930. The first part of the paper reads as follows:
This paper deals with an occurrence of radium ore near Wilberforce, Haliburton county, Ontario, upon which development work has recently been undertaken and which seems more likely to prove of commercial grade than any other deposit of radioactive minerals hitherto found in Canada. This occurrence is sometimes called the Richardson property, after Mr. W. M. Richardson, the discoverer, and will be so referred to in the present paper.
The ore is referred to in the paper as radium. At that time not much had been heard about uranium. Nothing was known about it so far as atomic energy was concerned. I want to bring it to the attention of the government that the ore was found some years ago. Then there is this passage in the paper:
The first discovery of radium ore in the Wilberforce district was made in 1922 by Mr. W. M. Richardson, a prospector and miner with Alaska and Yukon experience, who had come to Wilberforce in connection with the finds of molybdenite that had been made near that place ... In the course of prospecting the district, Mr. Richardson found a heavy, black mineral in surface outcrops of pegmatite at different points on the property, and having obtained a sample of . . . pitchblende, identified this mineral as uraninite. He, therefore, took up the mining rights on lots 4 and 5 in concession XXI, and on lot 4 in concession XXII, and proceeded to open up a number of small prospect pits and trenches.
A sample of uraninite sent by Mr. Richardson to Ledoux and Company, of New York, for assay, was reported by them to contain 58-35 per cent of uranium oxide .... equivalent to a radium content of 147 milligrams of radium per ton. Late in 1922, Dr. W. G. Miller visited the property and described it briefly in The Canadian Mining Journal of January 11th, 1924.
I mention that to show the house that what they were looking for at that time was not uranium. What was in their minds was radium which they wanted for medical purposes. Then I read the following from the paper:
In 1926, Dr. G. E. Richards, director of the department of radiology, Toronto General Hospital, had visited the property and secured samples of the ore and spring waters. With respect to the latter, Dr. Richards reported that three samples of water taken at various points all showed distinct radioactivity.
In 1927, Mr. M. D. Kennedy made a report on the property to the present company, who in 1929 commenced their first development work. Up to
The Address-Mr. Hodgson this time, attention had mainly been focussed on several outcrops of pegmatite that represented the points of original discovery of uraninite. . . . It is upon this lead that attention has since been centered and upon which work is proceeding at the present time. All of the three shipments of ore made to the mines branch in 1929, and upon which tests were run, came from this vein.
Since that time this paper was written, and late in the 1930's uranium was discovered there. As I said on Friday night, I do not think these people had very much encouragement from the government so far as uranium was concerned, but in spite of the government and the mines branch that property has been developed until today there are some 2,600 odd claims staked in a township and a half of that area. A lot of diamond drilling has been done and as soon as the snow goes in the spring much more diamond drilling will be started.
I might say that the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Eyre), who is interested in supplying diamond drills and equipment for hard rock drillers, took a stroll through that area last fall. Inasmuch as he has some experience in other mining areas, he certainly was not there to see me. At least, he did not call me. However, he did go over the area, and starting on the first day of April his company is supplying 7 different hard rock diamond drilling outfits in that area.
We have also had there some of the best geologists and engineers in the Dominion of Canada. Many of them come from the northern part of Ontario. There have also been many surveys made, maps prepared and so on. I hold in my hand a map of the district. You will see many other claims staked on it besides those in colour, but the coloured parts will give you some idea of the mines that are ready to operate. Some of them have already started and the rest are ready to begin in the early spring. I could not begin to give the names of all 2,600 companies but these are some with which I am familiar: Rare Earth, Tyson, Blue Rock, Homer Yellowknife, Faraday, Denfield, Croft Uranium, Centre Lake and Canadian Radium.
Quite a few of these mines are subsidiaries of other mines in Ontario. There is no doubt about it that the diamond drill holes now show that we have the goods in that area. Rare Earth has found three distinct rare minerals there, thorium, zirconium and hafnium. Columbium has also been found. These minerals are in quite large quantities and good percentages. That company is a private concern. Nobody is helping it, but it has 37 diamond drill holes below 1,000 feet and they have proved they

The Address-Mr. Hodgson have enough there in any one of these three claims to almost pay for operating the mine.
So far as uranium is concerned, there is a tremendous potential demand for uranium being created throughout the free world by the present research work on the applications of atomic energy both for military uses and industrial developments such as ship propulsion, electric power, etc. Present production goes exclusively to defence requirements and consumption figures are not available.
So far as other rare minerals are concerned, zirconium and hafnium, they are both newcomers to the industrial field and demand for both of them is expected to increase concurrently with the development of nuclear reactors. Zirconium has no substitute in the construction of nuclear reactor power plants on account of its physical properties, resistance to heat and corrosion, and low thermal neutron absorption cross-section. It is also very much in demand as a metal that can withstand the high temperatures in the combustion chambers of jet engines. According to the United States bureau of mines, as a structural metal, zirconium has tremendous potentialities.
Then we come to columbium. Columbium oxide also appears in appreciable quantity in the assay report. The most important use for columbium is the manufacture of high temperature steels and alloys used in jet aircraft engines. Other uses include electronic tubes, low voltage rectifiers, electrodes for welding stainless steel, and as an oxide in ceramics. The United States is entirely dependent on foreign supply for this metal, and over 97 per cent comes from eastern hemisphere sources, largely Africa.
I believe I am safe in saying, Mr. Speaker, that in Haliburton we have the makings of the greatest mining development that has ever occurred in Canada, as a result of the tremendous amount of uranium ore concentrates that have been found there as well as these rare metals. Whether or not these mining ventures have received very much encouragement from the atomic energy commission or the Department of Mines of this government, matters not. I am not going to argue about it. The people concerned seem to think they have had no encouragement whatever. If no consideration has been given to this company up to the moment I ask the minister, in all seriousness, to give some consideration to it because uranium cannot be mined without the approval of his department. This mineral has to be sold to the government according to the laws of


the land, and an export permit cannot be obtained without the approval of the Department of Trade and Commerce. In all sincerity I ask the minister to once more look over the situation. I am sure he will give it some consideration when he sees the assay reports from that area.
There is only one more thing about which I should like to say a word in this debate. When the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) was speaking a few days ago, he linked the trips made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to Quebec to those made by Sir John A. Macdonald at the time confederation was under consideration. I believe everyone will agree with me that the meetings attended by Sir John A. Macdonald resulted in Canada becoming one of the greatest countries in the world. I do not see how one could liken those trips to the trips made by the Prime Minister, and especially the last trip the Prime Minister made in September when he made a sword rattling speech. The Prime Minister took a different attitude when he went down to deal with Mr. Duplessis on the tax situation. Much to his credit, he is trying to do an about-face now. He is trying to patch up some of the mistakes he made in September. I hope the government will call a provincial conference as soon as possible, so that we may have more unity in Canada in the future than we have had in the past.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate on the speech from the throne, I feel highly gratified to share the opinion of those of my colleagues who have seen in this speech an important document, a harbinger of measures favourable to the stability and happiness of this country. It goes without saying that not everybody can attempt an analysis of the subject from the same point of view. Some see in this debate an opportunity for assailing the activities of the government of the country in order to promote the interests of their own party.
Such being the case, since the beginning of the debate, we have had occasion to hear the most surprising statements indeed. I was particularly struck by the description given of such an historic document as the speech from the throne by one hon. member who spoke of it as being a "desert of ideas in a flood of words". The hon. member felt justified in thus describing the speech made by His Excellency the Governor General on January 7 last.
Of course, it could not be given to all to possess to the same degree as the hon. member the art of striking out of a speech all

needless, superfluous words. For my part, I find in this document the outline of a concise doctrine that has been familiar to all of Canada for almost 20 years. Indeed, one only needs to reread the same speeches, made over the past 20 years, including that of 1955, to find in them the political philosophy which has made Canada one of the great countries of the world. I am happy to belong to the political party which has been the initiator of this philosophy of security and progress.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to concur in the splendid appeal made in this house by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robi-chaud) in favour of the bicentenary celebrations, which have started, in order to commemorate the deportation of the Acadians. I heartily endorse his invitation to all Canadians to join in those celebrations.
In order to further stress the character of these celebrations, I should like to quote briefly from a recent news item on the subject:
At first people might wonder that our friends in the maritimes should choose such a painful anniversary as an occasion for great rejoicings. On second thought, however, no occasion could be more proper. In the first place, this celebration has the great advantage to show all Canadians that there is no ill-feeling left among Acadians.
If they faithfully recall the past to honour the heroism of their forefathers they do not drift into sentimental memories. They prefer to study the present in the light of the future.
Acadians have faith in the future; they know from experience that they carry within themselves the necessary resources of courage, tenacity and clear vision that will promote their development.
WhUe they are proud of their religious and national beliefs, they are not at odds with the present. On the contrary, they are striving to achieve a significant position. Because of their devotion to their small Acadian motherland, theirs is an efficient contribution to the greatness of Canada as a whole.

In a speech made during the last session, Mr. Speaker, I mentioned that the economy of my constituency revolves around three important industries, namely, farming, fishing and lumbering. I would like at this time to refer again to these subjects. Figures of the 1951 census indicate that at that time we had in Kent county 2,328 farms. It is therefore evident that much of the economy of the country depends upon agriculture.
Farming conditions for 1954 were only fair. Unusually wet weather hampered farming operations considerably, and farm returns were greatly affected. These conditions were additional factors hastening the trend toward the desertion of the farming profession. I have had farmers come to me who were abandoning farms on which they had brought 50433-43
The Address-Mr. Michaud up large families, and who were going out to seek ordinary, unskilled labouring jobs.
In further analysing the above statistics we find certain classifications in connection with the farms in Kent county. We see that out of 2,328 farms, 538 are occupied by parttime farmers. We see that 604 farmers have incomes of less than $250 and that 622 have incomes between $250 and $1,199. Then, there are 405 farms on which the incomes are between $1,200 and $2,499, and 100 farms with incomes between $2,500 and $3,749. There are 30 farms with incomes between $3,750 and $4,999; there are 21 farms with incomes between $5,000 and $7,499, and three farms with incomes between $10,000 and $15,000. On only one farm is the income over $20,000. In the light of these figures it is apparent that the greater number of farms in Kent county are in the low income bracket.
I had suggested last year that, because of the peculiar local economic conditions, the Department of Agriculture should conduct an economic survey to ascertain the possibility of improving present conditions. I still believe that survey to be essential, and I wish now to renew my request, hoping that it will receive from the department the most earnest consideration.
May I voice to the government the hope of the farming population in my constituency that the policy of supporting the price of butter will be maintained. The dairy industry is basic to farming in Kent county, and we would view with apprehension the possibility of discontinuing this policy. We feel it would have an unfavourable effect upon the economy of our rural communities.
I would also express concurrence in the remarks delivered on January 12 by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy) with regard to the course followed by the Canadian farm loan board in our area. It would seem that this board has lacked on numerous occasions the flexibility required to fulfil its purpose. Too often loans which are really needed are refused because of a too-rigid system of assessment. More leniency therefore seems desirable in the application of an otherwise beneficial farm credit system.
I was pleased to learn in the speech from the throne that legislation is to be introduced to provide loans to fishermen similar to those provided farmers under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Although the full extent of this proposed legislation is not yet known, I earnestly hope that following its enactment loans will be made available to lobster fishermen, such as are found along the eastern shores of New Brunswick. Lack of credit facilities is often a serious handicap to many of these fishermen. Capital is sometimes required to build a new boat, buy a new engine,

The lumber industry in Kent county is of major importance. Wood cuts are chiefly in pit props and pulpwood, which, for the greater part, are shipped to outside markets through Buctouche and Richibucto harbours. Some 42 boats, carrying approximately 53,000 cords,


were loaded at Richibucto, and 28 boats, carrying approximately 42,000 cords, were loaded at Buctouche, during last season. These totals do not include, of course, the amounts shipped by rail, or through ports outside the county, nor the long lumber operations of the county. These different aspects of the industry give us an estimation of its importance to the economy of Kent county. Farmers, settlers, truck owners, stevedores, in large numbers, depend upon this industry.
I had good reasons, therefore, to be deeply interested in the speech delivered in this house last week, by the hon. member from Gatineau (Mr. Leduc), on the alleged pricefixing methods practised in the lumber trade in his area. I have had many people in my constituency complain about the abnormal situation of falling prices for the pulpwood or pit prop cord, beside an increased cost of living. The local producers, for the last four or five years, were compelled to accept steadily decreasing prices for their wood; this year again, they will receive $1 less than last year; $9 a cord compared to $10 a cord last year. I submit that this is barely more than the value of the labour involved for cutting a cord of wood, and the stumpage value. Newsprint, on the other hand, during the same period, remained on the upgrade. I was further interested in the declaration made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that an investigation into this matter will be pursued. In view of those circumstances, this investigation should also be extended to the part of the country I represent.
I want to express my satisfaction with the amendments recently brought to the Unemployment Insurance Act, Mr. Speaker. I know that this will be of great benefit in many instances. May I also express to the Department of Labour my hope of seeing the benefits of unemployment insurance extended to the fishermen of the country. This measure would prove of great assistance to many fishermen of my constituency.
In listening to the speech made in this house last week by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), I was delighted by his reference to a native son of New Brunswick who became prime minister of Great Britain. If New Brunswick feels proud of this distinguished son, we, in Kent county, feel doubly proud, because it was in this county, in the town of Rexton, that Bonar Law was born in 1858. He went to Scotland when still a boy. Today a cairn in the town of Rexton perpetuates the memory of a great man who, as a boy, lived in those quiet surroundings.

Mr. Speaker, when the speech from the throne was about to be read a little more than three weeks

ago, all Canadians listened with anxiety to what it might contain. Although some of us were pleased with some aspects of it, we were disappointed with others. For my part, I wish to say that it did contain several items which were pleasing to me, and it would be fair to say probably pleasing to most of the people in the maritime provinces. To begin with, it was noted that plans are under way to commence the building of a new ferry to connect Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia for the service which now exists between Wood Island and Caribou. It was also noted that a new ferry would come into operation this year between North Sydney and Port aux Basques, Newfoundland. Notice was also taken of the fact that a new ferry service will be inaugurated between Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, and Bar Harbor, Maine. We are all pleased to see these improvements in the transportation set-up in the maritime provinces. They should react beneficially on our economy generally because, if the cost of transportation can be reduced, markets will become more readily available for the producers in that area. It was also noted that very shortly the Canso causeway joining the island of Cape Breton with the mainland of Nova Scotia would be completed. That is a remarkable engineering achievement. It is perhaps unique in this country. But it is a thing that carries with it not only a blessing but also some disadvantages that will cause some inconvenience to groups of people as economic readjustment will be necessary when this new type of more rapid transportation between Cape Breton and the mainland comes into use.
However, we in Prince Edward Island, in common with the people of Britain, Bermuda, Newfoundland and various other places, are conscious of the peculiar advantage we have in being able to say that we live on an island, because living on an island has definite advantages. Island people all over the world have been leaders in their fields, generally speaking.

Be that as it may, I should like to run over the history of the Crowsnest agreement to show that it is not, as is commonly presumed, an agreement under which the railways are absolutely hidebound to maintain these rates. In doing this I am not presenting an argument to have the rates abolished. I am simply indicating that there should be some assistance from the treasury to make up what losses are incurred as a result.
It is all right for people to say that the railroads made this agreement, let them stick by it; that the railroads were subsidized when they were built across Canada; that they received land grants and millions of dollars. But the fact still remains that commodity rates do fluctuate on these lines and they must fluctuate, otherwise the railroads would be out of business. They are a very important part of our national economy and they must continue to operate. We should be ready to give them some consideration.
The historical background is that by agreement with the government of the time in 1897 a railroad was built between Lethbridge and Kootenay Landing. A subsidy of $11,000 a mile was paid, amounting to some $3,630,000, not a large amount. There is a fallacious argument currently being spread about that the Canadian Pacific obtained the great Sullivan mine as a result of their -agreement to build the Crowsnest pass railroad. But that is not so. Shares in the Sullivan mine were purchased with the funds that would have been otherwise used for expansion or for the payment to the shareholders of the railroad. It was not until about 1920, I believe, when the Canadian Pacific got into the mining business. From my point of view, and from the point of view of many, it was a good thing


that money was available at that time to develop this great industry of the east and west Kootenays.
At that time the company agreed to reduce rates on a great variety of articles moving eastward, articles such as farm implements, wire nails, fresh fruits and so on. Had this remained so, then perhaps we in British Columbia would not find our freight rates as high as they are today. Those rates were to be in perpetuity, but of course that was absolutely impossible.
The Canadian Pacific was of course the only railroad operating in the west at that time, and it agreed to lower the cost of shipping wheat to Port Arthur-Fort William by 3 per cent, so in reality the present rates are 3 per cent below what they were in 1897. Certainly in the face of rising costs this could not go on, and in July, 1919, the Railway Act was amended. The board of railway commissioners, as it was then known, was given the power to adjust rates when it was considered necessary. They did adjust rates. Grain was then part of their jurisdiction. Three years later, in June, 1922, a new act was passed and it was then that the rates on grain were set to conform with the Crowsnest agreement.
My time is short and I simply want to say that there is no use putting our heads in the sand and ignoring facts in order to justify something that is quite obviously incorrect. I am just asking the house to consider this proposal by Chief Justice Sloan. I realize that grain is an important factor in our national economy and that we must compete in world markets, but I fear that unless we do something like this to effectively reduce freight rates British Columbia will be almost excluded from the eastern markets. It is my opinion that the beneficiaries of this particularly low rate are the consumers of eastern Canada and consumers abroad.
In the few minutes that I have left I should like to compare these rates with rates in the United States and I shall take stations of about equal distances from the great lakes. The rate from Maple Creek to Fort William is 23 cents per hundredweight whereas the rate from Havre, Montana, to Duluth, which is within a few miles of the distance, is 73-4 cents a hundredweight. Not that this is part of my argument, but I think it should be remembered by some of the members from the prairie provinces when they compare the price of grain in Canada with the Chicago price. They should remember that they are not giving a true picture as to the relative prices. Those are just two shipping points, but similar

comparisons apply to westward movements. I do not say that the rates should be identical to those in operation in the United States, or that a subsidy should be based on these rates. I say that we should be prepared, from the federal treasury, to make up the losses so that the freight rates in British Columbia will not suffer, so that the commodity rates will not have to be measurably higher to make up for those losses and so that the employees of the railway companies may enjoy the same amenities of life as are enjoyed by those who are employed in other industries.

No doubt in the next year or two, they will be able to haul, with their diesel engines, about twice as many carloads of grain as they were hauling previously with the old steam engines. Thus I hope in the future the railroads will find that 50433-441
The Address-Mr. Thatcher their costs have been cut so substantially that they may be able to continue this agreement. Certainly before agreeing to any change I should like to see more tangible evidence produced by the railroads that they are operating under impossible circumstances.
This afternoon I should like to deal briefly with two specific subjects. On January 6 last, over the city of Moose Jaw, we had another near collision between an R.C.A.F. training plane and a Trans-Canada Air Lines plane. On January 10-I was not in the house at the time-the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) in answer to a question said he felt that reports of the incident had been greatly exaggerated. He went on to intimate, as I understand it, that he deemed our present air safety regulations to be fairly satisfactory. I feel that I must take exception to such a view, Mr. Speaker, and there are several facts I should like to lay before hon. members.
The house will recall that last spring the most terrible air tragedy in Canadian history took place over the city of Moose Jaw. The planes involved were precisely the same two types that were involved in the incident on January 6. Despite the fact that about 14 such incidents have been reported since the fatal crash a year ago, the minister still feels that the air regulations are satisfactory. It seems to me, however, that they could and should be improved.
As to the last incident, I notice that the view of newspaper editorials, as well as the official view, seems to be that the R.C.A.F. was largely responsible. The T.C.A. people particularly seem to take such an attitude, including the captain of the ship which was involved. Perhaps the R.C.A.F. was partly to blame. But personally I cannot help feeling that Trans-Canada Air Lines is not going to ensure the safety of its passengers over the Moose Jaw area, or over any other training area, simply by blaming the R.C.A.F. Certainly it cannot do so at least until the company itself has taken every possible precaution.
I should like to say this afternoon that in my opinion Trans-Canada Air Lines and the officials of the Department of Transport have been lax in taking certain elementary safety precautions. I admit quite frankly that in these matters I am a layman, but I have discussed them with R.C.A.F. officials in the Moose Jaw area. As a result of those discussions I have several proposals that I should like to give to the minister for his examination and consideration. If they are not feasible he will perhaps tell me why they are not.

The Address-Mr. Thatcher
In the first place I fail to understand why Trans-Canada Air Lines planes, when approaching the Moose Jaw area where there are sometimes dozens of military planes in the air at the same time, do not notify the control tower. If they would notify the R.C.A.F. control tower, the military planes could immediately be alerted. When the recent near-crash took place on January 6, the T.C.A. plane was flying four and a half hours late. As one R.C.A.F. official to whom I was speaking put it, "As far as we knew, that plane was somewhere over Vancouver". How can Trans-Canada Air Lines-whose primary consideration I know is the safety of its passengers-neglect to give such notification?
In the city of Moose Jaw for two and a half years Canadian Pacific Air Lines flight 61 has actually used the same airport as the R.C.A.F. When a C.P.A. plane approaches the airport, the control tower is notified. Immediately all military planes go south or north; they clear the air and they clear the runways. This system has worked out so well that since the airport was founded at Moose Jaw there has not been a single complaint from any C.P.A. pilot. I know that R.C.A.F. officials are willing-indeed anxious-to have a similar type of arrangement with Trans-Canada Air Lines. I therefore respectfully suggest to the minister that our safety regulations should be amended to require that Trans-Canada Air Lines pilots coming into a military training area notify the military control tower. That procedure is particularly necessary if the flight is delayed.
A second suggestion which has been put forward to me, and which seems sensible, is that Trans-Canada Air Lines planes, which normally travel at an altitude of about 6,000 feet, should go up to 8,000 or 9,000 feet when over a training area. I am given to understand that Harvard planes, or planes of that type, ordinarily do not fly at such a height. If this suggestion were adopted I think the possibility of a crash would be greatly lessened.
I would make a third suggestion, even though some of the authorities may not agree with it. On night flights some of the military authorities tell me it would be much safer if Trans-Canada Air Lines had more lights on the exterior of their planes. The blinker lights are sometimes a little hard to see, particularly if the weather is stormy.
Trans-Canada Air Lines is a wonderful company. However we are obliged to train NATO pilots and, whether we like it or not, I suppose we shall be obliged to continue to train pilots in the years ahead. While no regulations can be airtight, it seems to me
fMr. Thatcher.]
that someone should tell Trans-Canada Air Lines that we expect their pilots to do more than just set their course and then fly in a straight line. Until that something more is done I do not feel that Trans-Canada Air Lines are taking all possible safety precautions. I think if these steps were taken, it would increase the safety of air travel.
The second matter I should like to discuss this afternoon has to do with the announcement made last Thursday by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to the effect that the government is now prepared to sell butter to hospitals and other institutions, up to 20 million pounds I believe, at 21 cents per pound less than cost. I take it that this action could mean that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) may have to find about $4-2 million, if the whole quantity is sold. In many ways I think the Minister of Agriculture is to be commended for such an ingenious scheme. After all, butter is a perishable product and we cannot keep it indefinitely.
I notice that the Americans have been trying to dispose of their surplus by giving it away to foreign countries at cut-rate prices. I like the minister's proposal better. In this manner Canadians will get the benefit of the subsidy, particularly institutions which need it. At the same time I feel that this emergency step, which after all will be quite costly to the Canadian taxpayers, should cause us to re-examine our price support program for butter. I know that one hon. member after another taking part in this debate has urged the government to keep the present floor price on butter. I think the hon. member for Kent, New Brunswick (Mr. Michaud) made such a plea this afternoon. I also know that most members of the group to which I belong favour the government policy.
I wish I could be convinced in my own mind, Mr. Speaker, that the present floor price of 58 cents is a good thing for the producer. I may be wrong but, speaking only for myself, I fear that the floor price of 58 cents, which was originally introduced in good faith to help the producers, is not actually having that result. I ask hon. members to look at the facts for a moment. For the past several years our population has been growing by more than 400,000 people per year, but despite that fact the consumption of butter has been going down. In the same period of time the consumption of oleomargarine and other substitutes for butter has been going up by leaps and bounds. In other words, as I see the

The Address-Mr. MacEachen
problem the dairy producer is gradually being squeezed out of the domestic market.
What about our export market? Our export market for butter seems to have completely disappeared. I suppose the main reason is that the Canadian price is about one-third above the world price. I understand that New Zealand is laying down butter in Great Britain at approximately 40 cents a pound. I also understand that the Americans are considering dumping their surplus on the world market. Of course if they do that the world price will go down even further. To sum up the present situation, it seems to me that by virtue of our floor price the Canadian butter producer (a) has already been priced out of the export market and (b) is now being gradually squeezed out of the domestic market.
I fully realize that the dairy industry is very important. I think it employs about 17 per cent of our working people. I also realize that any sharp drop in the floor price of butter at this time would cause hardship. Yet the fact remains that the government's artificially supported price is today discouraging butter consumption at a time when we have a large surplus, and at the same time is encouraging the use of substitutes.
What should be done? The present government program has been quite costly to the taxpayer. I would not object to that if the dairy producer were actually being helped. Under these circumstances I think it would be a good thing, because I believe in reasonable support prices for farm products. But, as I see it, giving away butter to foreign countries or giving it away to hospitals and institutions can only be justified as an emergent, temporary solution to a difficult problem.
I think our dairy producers and the government simply must face certain hard economic facts in the country today. If our producers are to regain their market for butter, I do not see how it can be done other than by a reduction in price. I point out that last year President Eisenhower reduced the American butter floor price by a few cents, yet consumption of butter increased almost immediately by 7 per cent. As I say, speaking only personally, I believe that if a similar step were taken in Canada it would have the same result.
I wish to reiterate that I believe in reasonable floor prices for agricultural products. I believe that such floor prices are necessary for a stabilized agricultural economy. But where butter is concerned, the existence of substitutes has completely complicated the picture. I favour the retention of a sensible
floor price for butter; but I believe if butter is to compete, the level of that floor price must be reduced in the not too distant future.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish at the outset to associate myself with those speakers who preceded me in this debate in extending congratulations to the mover (Mr. Leduc) and seconder (Mr. Car-rick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
The contents of the throne speech have been fully discussed, and it is not my intention to repeat the deserved tributes paid to the measures it proposes for the consideration of the house. I derived satisfaction from the features of the proposed legislation which have as their object the strengthening of those safeguards against insecurity experienced by citizens of this country. Those of my constituents who make their living in the fishing industry will be gratified at the most welcome announcement that a new system is proposed for the improvement of the loan facilities available to fishermen.
Attention has been focused in the course of this debate on the impressive growth in the Canadian economy in the past decade. This growth has been reflected in a growing labour force, in an increased willingness to invest and, indeed, in an expanding volume of international trade and other signs of economic advance. Canada has a dynamic and expanding economy, and we all agree that continuous growth is essential not only to maintain the present standards of living but to provide for higher levels of income and employment opportunities for the Canadian people.
But it is also clear that an economy of growth is an economy of change; change through the appearance of new products which take the market away from older products, the discovery of new and more economic processes, the development of new resources and the putting into production of new inventions. This type of change has been termed in a broad sense technological development. But while technological change or development promotes the economic growth of certain industries, it does not occur without convulsive repercussions on other industries which must attempt, sometimes unsuccessfully, to meet new threats to their existence. Workers find their former skills no longer useful, and industries find their products no longer in demand. A dynamic economy will generally exhibit, simultaneously with rapid growth in certain sections, rapid and painful declines in other sections of the economy.
It should be the object of all interested in human welfare to attach greater importance to the undesirable effects of technological

The Address-Mr. MacEachen change. We should try to consider the most desirable methods to use to overcome the painful readjustments, and if possible to incorporate such measures into social and economic policy. Unless such efforts are undertaken, certain groups will be called upon to shoulder the chief burden of progress which is of benefit to the community as a whole.
As a member from Nova Scotia I wish to take notice of two cases where technological change, in a general way, is placing strains, and may place further strains, on groups and communities. The report of the dominion coal board, recently tabled in this house, painted a very disheartening picture of the Canadian branch of that industry. Members of the coal board expressed their concern in several passages of that report. One quotation, however, will be sufficient to illustrate the awareness of the members of the board of the present stress on the coal industry. The board states:
To all concerned or Interested in Canadian coal mining it has become forcibly evident that the Industry is presently facing conditions which threaten the very basis of its existence.
Those conditions threatening the very basis of its existence, in so far as Nova Scotia is concerned, can be briefly summarized. The first of these threatening conditions is the rapid rise in the pithead cost of mining coal in Nova Scotia. This rise is very disturbing. It amounts to $2.25 per net ton since 1949 for the major producer. Increasing production costs are, in my judgment, the principal problem to be faced in reaching proper stability in this industry.
It will be recalled that following an investigation into the coal industry conducted by the federal government, the Maritime Coal Production Assistance Act was adopted by this parliament. It was the purpose of this legislation to reduce production costs to the industry through the provision of loans for mechanization purposes. Much confidence was placed in this program as a means of permanent rehabilitation of the coal industry. Not only have the results of this program been disappointing but the chief operator in Nova Scotia, Dosco, has expressed doubt as to whether this program should be continued in view of deteriorating market prospects.
If mechanization, the installation of machinery, cannot be expected to lower production costs in the time and at the rate required, then an acceptable alternative must be found. The industry depends for its future on arresting the trend toward higher costs, and if possible effecting substantial reductions in present production costs. Otherwise coal will be unable to meet the competition

of fuel substitutes, and will be clearly unable to improve its market outlook. It is to these acceptable alternatives, Mr. Speaker, that I wish to direct a few remarks.
The predominant characteristic of Canadian coal mining is that the labour bill makes up the major part of the total production cost. At the moment the wage bill or, if you wish, the income to the worker is such that about 53 cents of every dollar spent on coal production goes to the working force. If a wider definition is taken of the wage bill, then 60 cents of each dollar goes to the working force.
I am not suggesting that wages in this industry are too great; far from it. This fact, however, namely the proportion of labour cost to total production cost, is suggestive of a solution. This means that the working force in the coal mines, if properly organized and activated, could effect substantial reductions in total cost through their ability to control the wage bill which is such a large share of the total operating costs.
I am convinced that if coal miners were given an opportunity to influence production decisions, improvement would definitely result. The miners and their families are those most vitally concerned with the welfare of this industry. Seldom, however, is any thought given to the best method of harnessing this great human resource for the rehabilitation of the industry. I suggest that the dominion coal board, management and trade unions could examine with profit those instances, of which there are now a growing number, where this approach has brought about the kind of atmosphere that is conducive to improving production efficiency.
Turning now to the demand side of the industry, there are a number of hostile factors in operation. First, the United States coal industry, our historical competitor, is succeeding in bringing down production costs. Second, there is the competition afforded by residual oil and natural gas. Finally, there is the dieselization of the Canadian National Railways which, according to the dominion coal board, will have reduced this market for Nova Scotia coal by 600,000 tons in a period of four years, and will have dissipated it completely in a short period thereafter. This policy, undertaken in my opinion without careful assessment of its effects on the Nova Scotia economy, and without satisfying the public fully as to the source of fuel supplies in the event of war, will take away a large number of jobs in the coal mines when it reaches its culmination.
It may be that the future will vindicate the type of industrial statesmanship that has unremittingly pursued this policy in order

to effect internal business economies. 1 am sure, however, that the coal miners of Nova Scotia and the communities dependent upon this industry are also correct in their claim that this program should have been undertaken more gradually. If it must be regarded as an inevitable policy, it should have been undertaken more gradually and not at a time when the industry was meeting adversity from several other directions. Here is a plain case where a technological change is imposing a burden on one sector of the economy, though it is to be sincerely hoped that the over-all effects will be thoroughly beneficial.
Faced with rising pithead costs on the supply side, the industry is meeting this stiff competition on the demand side for the reasons I have outlined, and all of them are attributable to the technological change occurring in our dynamic economy. While it is possible to separate the supply and demand side of this industry for the purpose of analysis, both features are closely interrelated if only for the reason that the chief determinant of the ability of the industry to compete successfully is this very important factor of cost of production.
Very telling evidence of the rapid changes that have overtaken the coal industry is the fact that the royal commission which examined this industry so exhaustively some years ago did not foresee the new technological and economic developments. The dominion coal board takes notice of this situation by the following comment:
However, new economic and technological development began to affect adversely the situation during 1952. It became evident that the Canadian coal industry was faced with problems which could not have been foreseen by the royal commission.
If new directives and new policy are to be shaped to meet new conditions-and I am not overlooking the important contribution the dominion coal board can make-then it might be useful to consider a new investigation of this industry, taking into account developments which began to become pronounced in the past two or three years. The only reassuring feature is that at the end of 10 years, so the experts claim, the fuel requirements of Canada can only be satisfied through increasing dependence on coal as a source of supply.
The interim period, from the present to that time of greater fuel requirements, will continue to be most difficult for this industry and the persons dependent upon it for a livelihood. The measures of government now in effect-the subvention policy and the
The Address-Mr. MacEachen Maritime Coal Production Assistance Act- may require strengthening to aid the industry over this period.
I now turn to another subject which is also in the category of change, in this case brought about to improve transportation facilities in Nova Scotia. This improvement was noted in the speech from the throne by the statement:
Since you last met Cape Breton island has been linked with the mainland by the new causeway which will be ready for service as soon as the ship canal has been bridged.
I am sure my constituents in Cape Breton island would have been more pleased if His Excellency had chosen to say:
Since you last met the mainland has been linked with Cape Breton island by the new causeway.
The completion of this project marks another step in the improvement of transportation facilities in the province of Nova Scotia. Though on official opening day its chief promoter in Nova Scotia, the late Premier Macdonald, will not be present to lead his 100 pipers into the county of Inverness, which was his birthplace and mine, there will be real satisfaction in the province as a whole to see his dream come true.
However, this new advance will affect detrimentally the three communities of Point Tupper, Port Hawkesbury and Mulgrave, contiguous to the causeway area. The chief source of employment in these communities at present is the rail and highway ferries operated by the Canadian National Railways and the provincial government from Cape Breton to the mainland. When these ferries are eliminated jobs will be lost, and unless quick action is taken a fatal threat will exist to the future of these communities. As the day approaches for the cessation of operation of these ferries, there is growing apprehension among the people concerned.
I do not believe that it was the intention of this government nor the intention of the government of Nova Scotia, when this project was inaugurated, that the citizens of these communities should bear the chief burden of an advance that will bring great benefit to the people as a whole. I believe further that when the action of any government is such that it threatens the jobs of any group of citizens, there is automatically created for that government an obligation and a responsibility toward those adversely affected.
I take note that the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway project will cause property damage or property loss, and I understand that it will be the desire to compensate for such loss. In our type of society job rights are as important as property

The Address-Mr. Montgomery rights, and on behalf of my constituents in the Canso area I must urge upon this house and the government the need for action.
However, the impression should not be left that the citizens in these areas have been reluctant to face up to the challenge presented by this problem. Some time ago the residents of the four counties affected organized themselves into the Antigonish-Guys-borough-Inverness-Riehmond development association and have undertaken a study and investigation of what industry would best replace the jobs now threatened.
The most promising project now under consideration is the establishment of a paper mill. At present I understand that several firms are interested, and the fruition of this idea depends upon the availability of wood supply and electric power. The forest inventory undertaken jointly by the federal and provincial governments is now nearing completion, and it is to be hoped that its findings will be favourable for this area. Such an industry would solve in large measure the problem of these communities. It would provide stability for the agricultural industry of the adjoining counties, and would usher in a new era of forest conservation.
I had the opportunity just recently to discuss this problem with the premier of Nova Scotia and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler), and on previous occasions with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters). I think it fair to say that all these hon. gentlemen expressed a real concern over this problem, and if I raise the matter again tonight it is because it is a matter of urgency where government responsibility must be recognized.
Mr. Speaker, I began these remarks by saying that the growth of our economy through technological development is necessary to maintain income and employment in Canada. Our search for further economic growth should proceed hand in hand with a full consciousness of the needs of those communities that will be affected adversely by developments that are in the general interest.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I would draw attention to the fact that some hon. members have taken on new responsibilities and assumed heavier tasks. I extend my congratulations to them and express the hope that they may be blessed with good health and divine guidance in the performance of their high office.
May I extend my congratulations to those hon. members who sit in the House of Commons for the first time. I trust they will enjoy their labours in parliament and their association with other hon. members. I would


extend congratulations, too, to the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe) upon the excellent job he is doing.
While the hon. member for Kent, New Brunswick (Mr. Michaud) is not in his seat, I would congratulate him upon his remarks this afternoon, because in them he set out clearly the agricultural picture in his constituency. I assure him that the picture he painted with respect to the county of Kent is one that could be painted for the whole of New Brunswick. I would stand behind him and support him in the advice he has given the government, particularly when he says that the Department of Agriculture should review why the agricultural economy of New Brunswick is at such a low ebb.
I would also like to back up the hon. member in what he said concerning the farm loan board, and that applies also to what the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy) said a few days ago; that when our farmers run into difficulties such as we have had in the past year, that just seems to be the time the farm loan board is not at hand, and the farmers cannot meet the regulations. In that connection the regulations concerning the farm loan board should be reviewed.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that the speech from the throne did not fill me with a great deal of enthusiasm. I did not detect anything in it that would be a shot in the arm for our agricultural industry, which seems to be in such a disheartening condition. I did not see any change in policy by which the declining incomes of our agricultural workers are to get any relief. There was encouragement, of course, in the speech from the throne, which I was glad to see, for certain groups and I shall refer to some of them. For instance, I fully support the amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act, and I hope they will meet the requests of the various members who have spoken in this house in the past, and of the Canadian Legion. The same remarks apply to the proposed amendments to the Blind Persons Act.
Another important piece of legislation was mentioned, namely the amendments to the Railway Act concerning the elimination of level crossings. I trust that these amendments, when they come down, will be broad enough to include underpasses, because there are many such in the country. I have some in my constituency, and there are several in New Brunswick, that are dangerous when one considers the number of vehicles and the amount of traffic on the roads. I hope these amendments will include underpasses as well as level crossings.
There are other items that I do not propose to take time to mention. However, in passing

I wish to say a word concerning unemployment. It is not a big problem in my constituency. The amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act which were passed recently will be helpful, and we are thankful for them. But I refer to a certain group of people, labourers, in my constituency and in other constituencies in New Brunswick, who are now unemployed and for whom no provision is made. When he spoke the other evening the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario (Mr. Hodgson) referred to this group.
I refer to that labouring group who depend upon farmers in the summer and who cut pulpwood and wood by the cord in winter. They do not seem to come under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Through no fault of their own they find themselves out of work, and there is no place to which they can apply for relief except directly to the municipality. I can assure you that the rural municipalities are not adequately equipped, nor are they in any financial position, to handle this problem satisfactorily.
Rural municipalities that depend upon agriculture are facing a gloomy year. Costs of production have not declined, but the incomes of those groups have been declining, and in addition to the normal trend in the decline of prices, owing to the excessive rain we had in New Brunswick last year a great deal of the crop that was planted last spring has never been harvested. That applies to hay, grain and potatoes, and a large percentage of the crop that was harvested was below average.
Therefore our farmers are not too happy about their position. This is naturally reflected in the financial position of the rural municipalities. All you have to do is read the papers and you will see that the financial reports of those municipalities at the year end invariably showed increased bank loans, increased tax delinquent lists, and larger budgets to take care of health, education, hospitalization and relief.
The labouring group to which I referred gets no assistance from the federal treasury. There is no way at the present time for the municipality to be reimbursed from the federal treasury. Judging from various speeches that have been made in this house we can all agree that unemployment is chiefly and primarily the responsibility of this federal government. But here is a group who are discriminated against, if you wish to put it that way. It does sound like a harsh word, but they make their living by labour. They do not come under the Unemployment Insurance Act, but they do get hungry when they get out of work. They need help, and they have to go to the parish and the municipality
The Address-Mr. Montgomery has to levy taxes directly on the people, which in rural agriculture areas are not easy to pay.
Some method should be worked out between the Department of Labour and the provinces so the municipalities, especially the rural municipalities, could be reimbursed for this type of relief. I just mention that casually because, while it is not a large problem in my constituency, there are quite a large number of people unemployed for whom there is no statistical record, and no record of which this house or the country generally has any knowledge.
I should like to pass on to another matter concerning the farmers. I do not think I am using harsh words when I say that the farmers in general are not getting their share of the producer's dollar, or of the consumer's dollar, whichever way you wish to examine the situation. A good many of them do not hesitate to say they feel that this government's trade policies are neglectful of their needs.
Many products have been mentioned, and I have a favourite one, too, which is potatoes. The hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) covered that ground very well; therefore I am going to curtail my remarks about potatoes. However, I do wish to say that I concur in what he said because I know he spoke in the interests of the potato farmers and agriculture in general down east. The potato farmers in the maritimes feel that they are in unfair competition with their United States neighbours.
I would like to go one step further than the hon. member went. I will give the house an example of just how unfairly the Canadian potato farmer is being treated under our present trade policy, in comparison with his United States neighbour. Within the last few days potatoes have been selling in Montreal for $2.60 per hundredweight. The American takes that $2.60, and because the Canadian dollar is at a premium it is really worth $2.67 to him. As the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) has explained to the house, it costs the United States potato grower nothing extra to produce potatoes for the Montreal market, but he receives 7 cents per hundredweight more than the Canadian farmer.
That may not seem much, but this is how it works out. It means an extra 4-2 cents on every bushel of potatoes. There are two different sizes of cars used to ship potatoes, one taking 700 bushels and the other about 550 bushels. In the case of the larger car it means $30 per carload which the United States farmer can take out of the Montreal market as a premium over and above what the Canadian potato producer receives.

The Address-Mr. Montgomery
I ask hon. members of this house if such a policy is fair to our Canadian farmers. By that type of policy the United States farmer is receiving protection on the Canadian market. We cannot expect the Canadian farmer to compete under those circumstances. I ask in all seriousness, as did the hon. member for Queens, that when trade agreements are being considered the eastern farmer and the potato farmer should not be forgotten. We do grow the best potatoes in Canada down there.
I am going to pass on to another subject, which concerns the obligation of the federal government to assist provincial governments in the development of natural resources. In speaking the other day the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) made out a strong case for assistance to New Brunswick in the matter of power. There is no need for me to review the case he made out concerning the immediate need of having cheap power available in New Brunswick in order that the people of our province may reap the greatest benefit from the development of our recently discovered base metal bodies, which are among the greatest on the continent.
Speaking in this chamber a little over a year ago I tried to impress upon this government the urgent need of having power available in New Brunswick at a lower cost. This province is already burdened with a debt which is beyond our ability to pay. What I said on that occasion still stands, except that I can now add the encouraging fact that surveys in my constituency, to which I referred, have shown that we have one of the most important manganese ore bodies in Canada or the United States. The latest information is that within the next 15 or 20 months a concentrate mill will be ready to go to work. They are going to develop that mine.
I am not speaking now about my own constituency, as this is a matter which cannot be confined to any particular area. It is our desire in New Brunswick, and I think I can fairly say that this applies to the maritime provinces, that we get the most out of what we have in the way of raw materials. It is our belief in New Brunswick that great advantage will be derived from these ore bodies if power is made available at a reasonable cost. If such power is available there is a possibility of a large smelter being erected in the Bathurst area. I am sorry the hon. member for Northumberland, N.B. (Mr. Mc-William) is not here, as I think he would back me up in this. If that smelter is established it is going to attract other industries such as producers of fertilizers, ammonium products, sulphur phosphates, potash products and

others. But the one thing that is needed more than anything else is power. We need assistance in order to be able to develop our natural resources.
I should just like to add that any national policy of assistance in the development of natural resources should permit a province to develop those resources which are the most beneficial. The only large power potential in New Brunswick is in the Saint John river basin. Although we hope there will be others in a few years, at present nothing else has been surveyed. The most important site there is the Beechwood site.
The most important item in connection with the development of this site is the cost, because that is what will determine the price to the consumer. I think it can be said that New Brunswick has lagged behind in industrial growth. We were one of the original partners of confederation. Without New Brunswick and the leading part played by the outstanding public men of that day there might never have been confederation. Whether it was right or whether it was wrong is not the question; the fact is that this original partner has not fared too well as a result of confederation. As a representative from that loyal and grand old province I feel that I need make no apologies when I come before this federal government and plead for help.
I am not asking for a handout on behalf of New Brunswick. Assistance does not necessarily mean a grant. But I would like the house to consider what central governments have done for other provinces during past years and what the present government is doing today for other parts of Canada. In the light of that, a grant toward capital expenditure would be nothing less than fair.
Especially is this evident from a survey or a perusal of the projects in which this government has helped other provinces, as enumerated by my friend the hon. member for Royal the other day. Others can be added. There was the St. Mary's dam. There was the large write-off to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta in the agreement writing down their debts in 1947. There was the assistance given to the railroads of this country to open up mining areas. There is also the big expenditure toward the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway, which was also mentioned by my hon. friend. Indirectly, if not directly, this assistance has helped to develop the resources of those provinces. It seems to me there is all sorts of precedent for it.
I agree, of course, with what the hon. member said the other day. I am not objecting, and we in New Brunswick do not object,

The Address-Mr. Montgomery
to the people in these other provinces getting this help because we can see that, bygetting that help, they have become better; the provinces have become bigger; they have grown faster; their industrial life is now of a higher standard. All we say is, give us some aid in the same way you gave them aid.
As I said a few moments ago, assistance may be given in various ways. If assistance is given to a province so it can develop its natural resources, it becomes a better member of the federal union; more revenue comes back to the dominion treasury; more work is provided. Just a few minutes ago we heard from the hon. member for Inverness-Rich-mond (Mr. MacEachen), who told us that the situation in his province, as a result of technological advancement, is not good and that he is looking to this government to do something. I think he has a right to do so. We in the small provinces must get assistance or we cannot afford to develop. It seems to me that one of the main functions of the central government is to look over the family in the union and help it here and there in order to keep all the members prosperous and keep the federation of provinces in something of a fair balance.
During the past two years our province has regained the confidence of the investing public. Nevertheless, for a small province such as ours to finance a large power development such as that which we need, at a reasonable cost, is a handicap. At the present time our capacity is approximately 105,000 kilowatts. I am informed that reliable engineers estimate that by 1959, just a mere four years from now, if we are to have development of these mines which we want to get, together with the natural growth of domestic use we shall require 215,000 kilowatts. I might add that those estimates were made before the last announcement of the discovery of this manganese ore.
There is just one thing more I want to add, and that is this. There is no secret about the fact-and it is accepted-that hydro can be developed at a cheaper rate than can thermal power, which is the only alternative. This so-called Beechwood site will develop 135,000 horsepower. It has been thoroughly investigated not only by our own competent hydro engineers but by such outstanding authorities as the Power Corporation of Canada, the consulting firm of H. G. Acres Company Limited and the Shawinigan Engineering Company Limited. It has been found to be feasible as a good power site, and a recommendation for its development is on paper.
This is not the only site that will need to be developed. Our power requirements are
going to grow. Thermal plants will have to be built. If the Passamaquoddy project ever becomes feasible the power produced will be needed by the state of Maine, the province of Nova Scotia and ourselves. Someone has said, "Why not wait for power to be developed by atomic energy?" I may say that I am reliably informed that it will take 15 to 20 years to develop power from atomic energy that will compete with hydro.
In the meantime what are we going to do? Are we going to sit down and allow all our raw materials to be shipped out for processing in the United States and other places? We need power now. We want it available in large quantities by 1957. We want that smelter in the Bathurst area. We want that sulphur extracting plant in the Newcastle area. We want those other factories that go along with them. We also want manganese to be mined and smelted in the Saint John river valley.
The other day my friend the hon. member for Royal pointed out that manganese is extremely important in the manufacture of steel. But what makes this ore body more important than others in Canada is this. Without the close proximity of sulphur for the processing, manganese cannot be smelted at reasonable rates. At the present time I understand that sulphur has to be brought in, and that the two minerals cannot be found close together. In New Brunswick we have them in close proximity. In my hon. friend's constituency of Northumberland, N.B., there is sulphur and in my constituency, which is a mere 50 miles away, there will be the manganese.
The fact that those two minerals are found so close together is going to make the project profitable and worth while. That is the information I have. This is why we want to be able to provide power for the smelting of those minerals. It is going to help our railroads and it is going to help our ports, not only on the Saint John but in the Newcastle-Bathurst area on the Miramichi. It is going to give many people work. It is going to make us in New Brunswick feel as though we have a rightful place in the economy of this country. Above all, it will provide many markets for our agricultural products here at home.
I see that not all the members for New Brunswick are in their seats, Mr. Speaker. I wish that they were, because I am going to extend an invitation to all hon. members from New Brunswick who sit in this house to speak up for their native province, to get behind this request on behalf of the people of New Brunswick, and to convince this federal government that we need this

The Address-Mr. Montgomery power and that we need their backing in order that the initial capital expenditure will not be too great. I am satisfied that the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Gregg), New Brunswick's representative in the cabinet, is doing all he can, but let us not leave it all to one man. I do not think he can do it alone, but by the united efforts of all members from New Brunswick, supported by members from our sister province, I am satisfied that the government will not only be convinced of the justice of our cause but will grant our request without delay. I am a bit surprised at the silence until now of hon. members from New Brunswick.
Including the minister.

I ask them, do you not want to see the people of New Brunswick share in the progress of Canada? Do you not want to see our resources developed to the greatest possible extent within the boundaries of our own province? Do you not want to see important smelters and other industries established at home? Do you not want to help our railroads and ports? Above all, do you not want to give the same opportunities to our young people at home as, in the last few years, they have had to seek in other provinces or foreign countries?
I am satisfied, if the request for assistance from the people of New Brunswick is not favourably considered by the government, that the people there will look upon the silence of hon. members from that province and the lack of a united front as one of the reasons such assistance was not forthcoming. Mind you, every consumer of electric power is interested in this matter, because the price at which power can be delivered to the consumer is going to mean a great deal to these people in the next few years. Everyone is an interested party.
If assistance in a material way in the initial stages of our power development is favourably considered and immediately advanced, in the next five years it will benefit nine out of ten families in our province. Not only will it do that, it will also benefit a great many people in our sister provinces because work will be provided for them too. It is no secret that negotiations have been in progress between the provincial hydro commission and officials of the federal government. I hope such negotiations will be satisfactory and helpful to our province, and that our people will be treated as people in other provinces have been treated in the past when assistance was needed. You know, it makes no difference under what name the aid is given. It all adds up to the same thing-assistance.
Finally, I join with the hon. members for Royal and Saint John-Albert, and those other

members who I hope will rise and take a stand on this matter before the debate is over, in sincerely and respectfully asking the federal government to give favourable consideration to New Brunswick's request for assistance in the initial development of hydroelectric power at Beeclrwood, which has been found feasible and has been recommended for immediate development. I am satisfied that a favourable capital set-up in the development of this project will be a means of helping the people of New Brunswick help themselves; and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that if they get that help they will be willing to go on.

Mr. Speaker. I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Leduc) as well as the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Carrick) on the fine speeches they delivered while moving and seconding the address in reply to His Excellency's speech. I do wish however to congratulate more particularly the electors of these two constituencies for choosing, as their representatives in this house, men who are so highly qualified and I have no doubt that they will fittingly represent their respective constituencies and render them, and their country, great service.
I am pleased to be in a position to congratulate the government and especially the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for the decision to sell, at reduced prices, the surplus 20 million pounds of butter to approved institutions such as schools, hospitals, old folks' homes, etc. I would like the same offer to be made to the Red Cross, to women's institutes, to houses of refuge or Sisters of Charity so as to help all these organizations which are of such great importance for the aged, the sick or the needy. After all, the government has to help them in any case. In this way, these less fortunate citizens would enjoy good butter, a product of superior quality which would replace all those substitute products they are being served now. You will no doubt have read with the same surprise as I did some statistics published in the January 26 issue of the Citizen. It was mentioned there that the Ottawa Civic hospital buys about 4,000 pounds of butter and 30,000 pounds of margarine annually, butter being served only to private room patients or those on a special diet. As far as I am concerned I should prefer that no margarine be used in hospitals. If they must use that product, then it should be in the proportion of 4,000 pounds of margarine and 30,000 of butter. In this way all the sick, the aged and the needy could enjoy butter.

Mr. Speaker, I have a suggestion to make to the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), which I believe would supplement the happy initiative that he has taken about butter. Here It is: he should buy five million pounds of cheese at the present price and resell it to these institutions, granting them a rebate of approximately 18 to 20 cents a pound, and then request that they serve good Canadian cheddar at all meals.
This same food product, together with a glass of milk, should be served free of charge twice a day in all our teaching institutions. For that purpose, I call upon our devoted and distinguished Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), who could negotiate agreements with provincial governments inviting them to pay 50 per cent of the expenses this would involve, while the federal government would pay the other half. This would improve the health of our school children.
To the right hon. Minister of Agriculture, to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), to our Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), as well as to the whole cabinet, I have another suggestion to make, one I have made in the past. In my opinion, the government should levy a sales tax of 10 cents a pound on oleomargarine and on all other butter substitutes. In return, the government could grant to all creameries a 10cent subsidy per pound of butter and maintain the ceiling price, of 58 cents a pound, for butter, to dairy farmers. With the storing costs, which average about one cent a pound, butter would then sell to wholesalers from 48 to 50 cents, according to the cost of transportation and storing, and the latter would have no right to retail butter at more than 51 to 55 cents a pound, according to costs of transportation and storage.
In this way the consumer could get butter at 10 cents less a pound. This tax on margarine would serve to cover part of the expense and the less fortunate among us could buy good butter very cheaply. Canadians could buy an excellent product while helping the farmers of this country and the charge on the government would not be excessive. That is very important, for it must be remembered that, if our agricultural class is not prosperous, the effects are felt throughout our economy. Our farmers are the heaviest buyers, per capita, of manufactured goods, for example of building materials or materials used in the repair of houses, barns, sheds, pig sties, chicken coops, garages, silos, fences and bridges, or again of farm machinery, automobiles, tractors, furniture, etc.
Certain hon. members would no doubt be surprised to learn that $6,000 worth of agricultural machinery of all kinds is required to
The Address-Mr. J. O. Gour farm 100 acres, and that any farmer who wants to buy a complete set of modem machines, such as combine, baler, ensilage cutter, milking machine or refrigerator, must part with $12,000 and more. Then too the farmer needs house furnishings like any village, town or city dweller.
If I am saying this, it is not because the constituency of Russell, which I have the honour to represent, is rural. On the contrary, though it has been rural, it has become 75 per cent urban. No, I am speaking in this way because I think that it is for the good of all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage). We are proud of him and of the fine work he has done so far.
I think too I should congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for his acumen in choosing his ministers.
Like other members, I regret the departure of some ministers, these most distinguished and qualified men, such as the Hon. Lionel Chevrier, former minister of transport, the Hon. D. C. Abbott, former minister of finance, and the Hon. Brooke Claxton, former minister of national defence.
However, our great and noble Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), guided by divine Providence, made a choice of other ministers who, in my opinion, will prove to be an asset to the whole country.
I should like to suggest to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) that he step up his reforestation program. In my opinion, the amounts devoted to this purpose by the federal government should be increased fourfold, and provinces should be requested to do likewise, besides getting county and township councils, as well as individuals, interested in reforestation and water conservation. I previously explained this here when I suggested a plan for the conservation of the water of the South Nation river which flows through about 15 counties in the eastern part of Ontario, making what is called the Ottawa valley.
I wish people who practise reforestation were exempt from land taxes; further, the money they spend on reforestation should be deductible from income tax, when they are called upon to pay it. These forests should be inspected by experts appointed by both federal and provincial governments and when time came to fell the trees these experts would point out the trees to be felled, as well as the trees to be replaced at that time. The owner of timber land could
