Mr. Speaker, I would feel remiss in my duty if I did not call attention to the insult uttered against the province of Quebec by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier). Although I do not live in Quebec, my constituency is adjacent to that beautiful province and I have several relatives, even brothers and sisters, among those charming Quebec people.
I have visited that province from one end to the other, as I did for all the rest of Canada, except for Newfoundland, where I would like to go shortly, because judging from the congenial and intelligent members sent to Ottawa to represent that province, I know that I shall not be disappointed.
I must tell my hon. friend from Burnaby-Coquitlam that he is completely ignorant of the character of the Quebec people, because there are no better, more intelligent and hospitable people in Canada. True, there are always some black sheep and I am wondering whether a few such from his own province are not now in Ottawa. If the present premier of Quebec has chosen to stress different points or give different interpretations of autonomy in order to have his candidates elected, a tactic of which I personally disapprove and which is certainly detrimental to good understanding and nefarious to the province of Quebec, it does not mean that he is a bad Canadian.
Does not each province and each political party have its own way of conducting elections and of submitting its program? Yes, Mr. Speaker, even the province of Ontario, one of the finest, not only in Canada but in the whole world, is inhabited by honourable, peaceful, intelligent and honest citizens, the great majority of whom are of English descent. I recognize that there are also some black sheep among them, just as there are in the maritimes and in western Canada. During my trips across Canada, I met honest, kind and intelligent people everywhere. This is not the place to disparage one province


or another. We are indeed fortunate in living in the greatest country in the world. In fact, we are truly privileged in having good citizens, from Vancouver to Halifax, and in Newfoundland-people who are the descendants of almost every race in the world, and who wish to live in harmony. The good I have to say about the other provinces, I also wish to apply to Quebec, where racial and religious matters, school rights and the rights of minorities are treated with more fairness than anywhere else in Canada. I would ask all hon. members to urge their own provincial governments to imitate Quebec as far as justice towards minorities is concerned.
Mr. Speaker, I would be angry with myself if I did not speak of the matter so often discussed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), namely divorce, to which I am absolutely opposed. Marriage cannot be likened to an exchange of houses or automobiles. Divorce is the ruin of the family. What happens to the children of divorced people? Divorce is a moral evil which is greatly detrimental to the country. Married people should learn to put up with each other, to live together and bear their cross. Of course, when people do not want to understand each other, it is easy to find means and ways of divorcing. Most often, men are the guilty parties.
But, since our legislation permits divorce -and I congratulate Quebec and Newfoundland for not accepting that legislation-and since as Canadian citizens, people in those provinces are entitled to submit their case to the federal government, in my opinion no court could settle those cases better than the Senate and the House of Commons. The Senate committee, where the requests are first dealt with, is made up of Canada's most honourable citizens, lawyers, notaries, doctors, businessmen and farmers, men devoted to public service, who have wide experience as far as race, religion and all classes of society are concerned. They know the laws and customs of the land, and are, in short, honourable men, since they have been chosen to sit as senators, independent for life of politics and the powers of finance. No abler group of men could be found to pass on matters of divorce. They have all the time they need to review such cases, since we sit from six to eight months a year. For my part, had I a case to be tried, I would be happy to submit it to the senators. I am convinced that those who apply to them obtain justice.
I would also like to thank the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) and the government for the improvement made to the airport at

Uplands and for their decision to spend over $3 million to make this an ultra-modern airport, something which is quite called for in this national capital of ours.
I also wish to thank the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) for his decision to build a military hospital at a cost of about $9 million at Billings Bridge. As it is the location of the Rideau health centre for ex-servicemen it is extremely well chosen. It provides all the necessary comforts to our convalescing veterans. Canada owes them all that can be done for their benefit.
While I have brought this matter to the attention of the Hon. Brooke Claxton, then minister of national defence, and of the present minister (Mr. Campney) on more than one occasion, I wish to come back to it today, in the house. I repeat that there are no better locations, with all the required space and protection from atomic attack, for the proposed national defence headquarters than the township of Gloucester, in the constituency of Russell. There are so many favourable sites that I shall refrain from singling one out. I am of the opinion, in any event, that in addition to the factors I have already mentioned, there is there all the space necessary to build houses for the employees who would like to live close to their work. This could be done at reasonable prices and I am sure that lots there would sell at one-tenth the price of those in centre-town.
We are certainly in need of housing, as evidenced by the fact that in 1954 the population of the constituency of Russell increased by 5,000, including 3,605 in the section annexed by the city of Ottawa.
I wish to congratulate the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) for the great improvements he has achieved in his department by providing a much better postal service. We are glad to have so well qualified and devoted a minister. However, I should like to make a couple of suggestions to him. First, he should so change the regulations that where 10 per cent of the population is English-speaking or vice versa, the postmaster be bilingual. At the present time, the regulation lays down 20 per cent for this privilege. This change would make for better understanding and facilitate the harmony existing between the two great races in this country. My second suggestion concerns postmasters, who receive salaries ranging from $500 to $900 annually, while supplying the premises and catering to the public for 8 or 9 hours a day during
Privilege-Mr. Dupuis
6 days of the week. I suggest they be given better salaries. Employees of the Post Office Department and myself will have great difficulty in finding premises and employees ready to accept such employment in my constituency. At the present time, some of these offices have been closed for two or three months in my constituency. In fact the last one closed has been so for more than three months and we could find no one to accept the salary offered by the department.
In conclusion, I should like to ask the Postmaster General and all the other ministers who have to decide on sites for the construction of buildings for their departments to pick sites in the constituency of Russell where they will be welcome and where they will find the localities best suited from all points of view.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is one matter with which I wish to deal briefly before saying anything on the speech from the throne. This is a matter which I am sure will have the support of all hon. members from the province of Saskatchewan, irrespective of where they may sit in this house. I refer to the jubilee celebration of the entry of Saskatchewan and Alberta into confederation.
Fifty years ago these two prairie provinces were admitted as constitutional members of the Dominion of Canada. We are proud of Canada, proud of its record, proud to belong to Canada and to be counted as citizens of this great dominion. Our story of the prairies is one of the moulding together of a cosmopolitan group of people from almost every country of the old world, from Europe and Asia. It is a story of how they pioneered that land together, met and overcame the difficulties and the problems of developing it into great provinces making a great contribution to the Dominion of Canada.
This year we are celebrating the fiftieth anniversary, and I merely want to say that Saskatchewan invites everybody in Canada, including all hon. members who can possibly come to that province this year, to visit the prairies and help us pay tribute to the great pioneers, those people who through their toil and courage have given to the people of Saskatchewan and Alberta, and Canada as a whole, a great heritage and a great example.
The throne speech of 1955 has been called many names. It was aptly described by one journalist as a rather dull chronicle of stale news. As a matter of fact it is, I believe, a masterpiece of evasion and indifference in so far as basic remedies for those economic problems which face Canada today are concerned. It seemed also to be studied in its efforts to pass over lightly some very important problems such as unemployment and the


declining farm income, things which face the Canadian people as a whole and which so often seem to be so far from this chamber.
Last year the same attitude was evident, and we attacked that attitude. At that time we asked that steps be taken to take care of the situation. We were told that unemployment was just seasonal and would rectify itself when summer came and the ice moved out of the great lakes and the St. Lawrence river. But this winter unemployment is even worse. In that portion of Canada from which I come the unemployment situation is at least 50 per cent worse than it was a year ago. The 60-day extension of unemployment insurance benefits, which everyone in this house supported and endorsed, is just a salve to help those unfortunate unemployed people through a couple of bad months in the winter time. It is no substitute for employment.
The people are eagerly looking for something to be done to assure them of some possibility of exchanging their labour for a living. Every trade union brief presented to the government in the past year has emphasized the matter of unemployment, yet no effective measures seem to have been taken. As a matter of fact, I personally am beginning to doubt whether this government has a cure for the problem short of a threat of war.
Policies dealing with trade and price control, which affect the cost of living, the problems of taxation and immigration-all these things affect the Canadian economy. They are the responsibilities of the federal government. The provincial governments can do very little about them; but if as a result of these policies half a million people are unemployed, then the responsibility for employable unemployed rests upon this government whose policies to a large extent have created the situation.
Instead of accepting that responsibility, what do we find? The government says to the municipalities, "We take no responsibility for the unemployed employables beyond the Unemployment Insurance Act". Is it going to be a repetition of the old story; that the municipalities are going to be asked to share this burden, with small grants from the provincial government, and they shall have to carry it?
That is just not good enough. The federal government receives approximately 72 per cent of the taxpayer's dollar. This government is responsible for the policies which largely cause unemployment in this country; and I repeat, this government must accept

The Address-Mr. Castleden
that responsibility. The convention of mayors of Canada pointed this out to the officials of this government. I can assure the government that unless they take more effective action to restore employment in this country there will be a storm of protest from all parts of Canada, and it will be a united protest. Half a million unemployed is not a healthy sign in a country such as Canada, with all its resources. Since the war we have brought a million people to this country. We heard members this afternoon tell of young men in their province going as far away as New Zealand in order to obtain employment in the lumber camps of that country.
When people are unemployed for any length of time they are confronted with serious problems. A man may have invested his life savings in a home, or he may be building a home. If unemployment strikes for a few months he can carry the burden, but when it continues beyond that length of time and he finds he must move away from the district in order to get employment, -if he can find it-he stands to lose his whole investment. It is a much greater loss than just being unemployed. It is too serious a thing to be taken lightly. It is a serious reflection on our economy that people can enjoy prosperity and employment only in wartime. If our economy cannot provide employment for the Canadian people it must stand condemned.
In the field of agriculture we have the same problem. In the presentations made to the government by various farm organizations, by the federation of agriculture, by the farm union organization, which is a growing, young and vigorous organization trying to unite the farmers so that they can speak with one voice, reference is made to some of the things which are basically wrong. They ask the government to take steps to remove some of the injustices and give some stability to the agriculture industry of this country so they can look forward to making a living in that industry. This is an industry upon which a large percentage of Canadians depend for their existence.
There is one thing common to all these protests. They state that their costs of production are continuing to rise while the returns for the things they produce and sell are constantly and rapidly declining. There can be only one final result if there is a continuation of that trend. When your returns keep lessening and your costs of operating continue to rise, as soon as they cross one another you are facing bankruptcy. They are facing this problem seriously; they are looking for some effective solution.
In many provinces of this dominion agriculture is the main industry. I believe it is safe to say that in our province over 80 per cent of the people obtain their living from agriculture. Unfortunately during the past year we were faced with a serious problem created by rust, and then frost. The income of the farmers of that province was reduced last summer by some $300 million. This is bound to have its effect upon the whole economy. Taxes cannot be paid; the provincial government is going to suffer from lack of income, it and municipalities are going to be unable to provide services to the degree they have in the past.
The farmer is trying to obtain some stability. He does not mind facing the ordinary difficulties with which nature may confront him. He has been brought up on that kind of thing, and he does not mind facing it. But he wants to know that if and when he does produce a crop as a result of his efforts, he can look forward to obtaining a proper return for his labour. If that is established, then he can weather the storms of a year or two of difficulty.
I was interested in reading the recommendations contained in the submission to the government of Canada by the interprovincial farm union council. They made reference to the difficulties which the western farmers were having in making both ends meet, and on page 3 of their brief they stated:
According to the federal bureau of statistics, from July, 1951 to October, 1953, the wholesale price index of manufactured goods declined by 15*6 points (1935-39=100). But the farm products wholesale price index dropped by 68-6 points in the same period-a difference of 53 points. This trend of falling farm prices has continued in a lesser degree during the remainder of 1953 and for 1954.
Farm people themselves, and those who are familiar with agricultural conditions, cannot help but be disturbed by diminishing farm income compared with abnormally high operating costs. Measured in terms of purchasing power-as represented in cash obtained from the sale of farm products-the farm dollar is worth less than it has been for a good many years.
It is to this that the farmer looks. He wants it done now, rather than having to wait. Each year creates new problems and makes it more difficult. A man finds he is going deeper and deeper into debt as a result of his operations. Unless there is some assurance of the forward pricing of commodities, unless there is some hope that he can plan his production so as not to lose more by going into production, the farmer will find himself in difficulty at almost every turn.
He is told that with hogs bringing 32 cents he should be feeding his grain to hogs. He goes into the raising of hogs; then a few months later when he brings the bulk of his
698	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Castleden hogs to market he finds there has been a decline in price and instead of 32 cents it is down to 20k cents. The price is below what was supposed to be the floor price. A break of 30 per cent is just not good enough. That drop of 30 per cent wipes out any possibility he may have of getting some return for his labour.
There are floor prices but many of them are too low, as was pointed out in this brief. Frequently a price is fixed for A hogs, but there is no floor price under the others. The spread between them constantly varies, and becomes so great that the production of second and third grade hogs means practically losing money. This is also pointed out on page 10 of the brief, where it states:
The government guarantees 38 cents per dozen at point of storage to those who store eggs, and for all practical purposes this is the end of the guarantee. Consequently, the producer receives whatever price is paid by the egg stations and we doubt very much if the country dealers will pay 32 cents a dozen to producers, as the Minister of Agriculture suggests they should.
The thing that is needed here is a guarantee to the producer, not just the packing company. Consumers know this as well, but farmers note that in spite of the deep decline in the prices they are getting for livestock- in 1951 you got $240 or $250 for a good steer which today can be bought for $100, a drop of almost 60 per cent-there is no corresponding drop in the price the consumer pays in the butcher shop or which the butcher pays when he buys his meat from the packing company. It is quite evident that the packing companies are able to manipulate prices for their own benefit.
The farmers' union have been unanimous in their requests that these injustices be removed. The request has been made year after year that a livestock marketing board be established to remove these injustices. This livestock marketing board should contain proper representation of farmers. The failure of the government to take more effective action along this line contributes a great deal to the discontent among the farm population. The trade unions have shown in their briefs to the government that they realize that a healthy agricultural economy is the best guarantee they can have that there will be a home market for the goods which they are producing. It means work for them in the farm implement plants. Automobile, truck and motor plants will continue in operation, and there will be work for them only when there is farm demand.
For some years now the Canadian farmers have been watching with envy the achievements of the United States farmers in the field of forward pricing, what they call 90 per cent


of parity. They recognize that there are difficulties in following the same kind of program in Canada where we export such a large percentage of our wheat. There is, however, one thing they realize. That is that if in other countries some floor can be placed under agricultural products to the extent that the farmer is given stability, through this system of knowing what his price will be when he goes into production, it is something he is after in Canada, taking into consideration the problems that face him in this country.
There should be some more adequate stabilization of farm products in a forward way so that, for instance, when the farmer starts into production in raising a herd of cattle, if that is going to be his business or if that is the business for which his land is best suited, he can go into it with some assurance that there will be a floor price below which his commodity will not fall; and that floor should be high enough so he will not be forced to spend years working on his product and then, when he comes to sell it, find that everything has dropped and that he is losing out.
The farmers in Canada are realizing their position. There is a new idea growing among them. That idea is that if our great neighbours can work together with their farmers so that all political parties support a program that will guarantee stability to the agricultural industry, then we in Canada can do the same thing. The farm organizations are asking the farmers today-whether they are in Alberta, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Ontario or Quebec-to come together in one organization so they can speak with one united voice to guarantee stability to an industry which I believe is the greatest in Canada, and upon which the prosperity of this dominion depends more than any other.
The importation of millions of pounds of cheese into Ontario at this time, without adequate steps being taken to protect the cheese producers, is just the type of thing that aggravates the farmer to the point where he is willing to kick over the traces. He wants to know where he stands with regard to policies of this kind. He wants to know where he will be with guarantees; if guarantees were given, would the government then assure him that if they import this cheese-if through some negotiations on the exchange of goods and trade this is necessary-he will know long enough ahead so he can take steps to adjust his production and the matter can be taken care of.
The farmers of Ontario who are raising stock find the same kind of problem facing them that faces the stock grower in western Canada. As these farmers get together they

notice that they too are being stymied every time they attempt to work together to stabilize the production of hogs or to get their commodity to the market. In some parts of Ontario the farmers, endeavouring to get truckers to haul their hogs from their own farms to their own packing plant, have found that the truckers, who are apparently under the control of the packing houses, refuse to haul their hogs to the market which the farmers designate. There are always the boys on top, one move ahead of the farmers, always keeping in control. They are afraid that the farmers, through their organization, in some way might be able to meet the kind of competition presented by the methods the packing companies use to beat them down.
The farmers of Canada are resolved, united and determined. They are not going to give up this battle until there is a proper program of stability for agriculture. You can hardly blame them. Certainly the people who for their own prosperity are dependent upon the farmers' prosperity, are going to support the farmers 100 per cent. The people who are in the farm implement business, the people who are dealers and merchants in the towns in areas and communities where their whole livelihood depends upon the prosperity of the farmer, are going to support him in getting a solution to this problem.
There is every indication that this country will be facing a tremendous bill for relief if the present trend continues with regard to unemployment. There is nothing today to indicate that the government have solved the problem. It is our contention that it would be much better for the government to spend money upon this farm industry in order to give it stability so these people can then get employment. Then they will not have to be paid for sitting idly and doing nothing. The money spent on a properly established price support program for farm products will, in our opinion, be much better spent than money spent on unemployment relief.
A healthy agricultural industry will do more to bolster the Canadian economy than will millions spent in a niggardly way in order to feed unemployed people. The farmer with income purchases farm machinery, furniture, automobiles, trucks, fertilizers, gas and oil, and equipment for his farm operations. His farm production provides work for railways, the meat packing industry and steamship lines. Canada will never sink into a serious depression as long as the farm industry has stability. The objective of all organized farmers in Canada is stability. They should have the support of all in this house in this demand for justice.
The Address-Mr. Castleden
To refer to my own constituency, may I say that the average farmer in my area operates a farm of about half a section or about 320 acres. His income this year will not begin to cover his 1954 operations. It is not unusual for the Canadian farmer to face calamity such as rust and frost and he is taking it without much complaint. But one thing the farmer demands is that there shall be stability next year when and if he can produce a crop. In the meantime some interim and final payments on the 1953 crop will help tide him over. It will not meet the costs. The farmer was in debt last year.
One year ago I pointed out the dangers facing agriculture, with declining income and increasing costs. At that time I told the house that the farmer had only one way to go and that was into debt, and that the farmer was going into debt. My statement was questioned here. I made personal contact with some of the people concerned and obtained corroboration from the local merchants, bankers and municipal officials. My own findings were that over 80 per cent of the farmers engaged in the agricultural business in my part of the province were in debt, some of them seriously. The situation will probably be worse next summer because the effect of the loss of the 1954 crop will not be felt until this next summer. This is the cause of the demand of the farmers.
In studying their problem the farmers see that they face an impossible situation by reason of this present situation. They have borrowed money to buy implements. The Farm Improvement Loans Act has been of some assistance to them, but they now find difficulty in meeting their obligations. One hope they have is that there is going to be some stability behind their operations in the future. Through their organizations, united in the western provinces at least and growing in the east, they have put forward to the government the things they feel to be necessary to achieve that stability. They are going to continue that fight, and the people who represent them here will be negligent in their duties if they do not support them.
Another thing that adds to the aggravation of the farmer is the continuance of the control over the allocation of box cars. When the farmer goes to deliver his grain it makes him very angry to find that he is faced with the necessity of delivering his grain to the opposition line elevator company merely because there was no allocation of cars to his own elevator. Every farmer should have the right to deliver his grain to the elevator of his choice. Surely that can be arranged at this time, when the heavy box car congestion is largely over. Any farmer who wishes

The Address-Mr. Castleden to deliver to the line elevator company should have the right to do so. The farmer saw that last year his wheat pool lost some 8 per cent, or 32 million bushels of grain in the handling operation because of the allocation of box cars.
This was an injustice which cut him very deeply. He fought for years and years to establish his own co-operative pool organization to fight against the organized grain trade and the grain exchange in Winnipeg which exploited him for so long. He finally established his own wheat board, and it disturbed him no end to see that these people he has fought against are now again gaining sufficient influence in high places to carry on this kind of campaign against his organization. He is going to continue to fight for his right to deliver his grain to his own elevator.
I should like to turn to another matter which is important to my constituents, and which was not mentioned in the throne speech. I refer to old age pensions. Our senior citizens are experiencing hardship and suffering which to say the least is disturbing. Before the present session is finished the government will be urged to increase the old age pension and the pension to the blind in keeping with the cost of living in Canada. When the old age pension was increased to $40 a month that was a good thing. We thought we were moving forward, but at the same time the government removed price controls and the increase in the cost of living just about wiped out the increase in the amount of the pension. Today $40 scarcely buys what $20 did 12 years ago. Surely something should be done to increase the amount of money paid to our old age pensioners, our senior citizens who are unable to earn a living any longer themselves and who have to depend entirely on the old age pension.
The pension should be related in some way to the cost of living in Canada, so that if the cost of living rises the pension will be increased by a proportionate amount. Thus these people would have some guarantee of their ability in the future to live on the pension which is paid to them. It is surely only right to these deserving people. Surely we can tell them that they will not be allowed to suffer as the result of a fluctuating cost of living. Canadians cannot be proud of this condition existing among the older citizens today.
Finally I want to refer briefly to the international field. In our efforts to win the world for democracy we must consider the hungry peoples of the world. It is necessary for us to prove by our actions that democracy is better than any other form of government,


that democracy means more to the people of the world than any other way of life. We now have the opportunity to help the hungry peoples of the world, particularly the millions of Asia. It is my belief that providing these people with food, and helping them to develop their own resources, is at least as good a way of wooing them to democracy as a show of military strength. In the world of today a police force is necessary, but at the same time a larger share of the expenditures of the government should be made for humane purposes. We should be helping to feed these people and expand the Colombo plan in order to show the world that the democratic way of life is the best way of life.
Since war is now the way to complete destruction it is evident to people that there must be some alternative to war. If there is, we have to change. Let us see that we change in the right direction toward tolerance and human brotherhood, rather than showing the mailed fist as one means of forcing our will upon our fellow men.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate with the intention of using most of my time to take advantage of the opportunity which this debate offers to discuss some of the problems of my own riding.
I represent the riding of Humber-St. George's, which in the last parliament was represented by Mr. W. R. Kent. I should like first to give you some facts about my riding. It comprises practically the whole west coast of Newfoundland, or that part of the province which faces the gulf of St. Lawrence. This riding includes three of the provincial electoral districts, namely St. George's, Humber and St. Barbe. It has a coast line of about 300 miles as the crow flies, but taking into account all the bays and indentations it is more nearly 1,000.
The St. George's area, which is in the southern part, is one of the beauty spots of the province, in fact one of the beauty spots of the whole of Canada. Farming is the main industry here and has been for a number of years, for here are situated some of the finest farms in the province. It may well be that with a progressive farm policy and fuller use of existing farm legislation on the federal level, a more vigorous marketing scheme could be encouraged as well as an increase in dairy and meat products. Logging and fishing are important to the area.
The fishing industry is one that has a potential well worthy of consideration. Cod and halibut are in abundance a few miles offshore, with the inshore fishing consisting of lobster all along the coast and with great

quantities of herring and scallops in Port au Port bay. But the task of the fisherman here, on a straight bluff shore with few harbours, is indeed one of many hazards. I hope we are not too far away from the time when facilities will be installed at Codroy harbour, Grand Bay, Port au Port bay and St. George's bay, not only for the sake of the fishermen in the area but also as a haven for the many small boats which ply their trade along the hazardous coast line. The middle section of my riding is known as the Humber, named after the Humber river which flows down the beautiful and fertile valley between thickly wooded hills to empty into the bay of Islands.
Here in this valley is another of the really good farming areas in the province. My previous remarks concerning farming would apply to this area, too. While farming has never been the major industry of Newfoundland I believe it could still play a greater part in the economy of the province than it has heretofore.
Along the shores of the bay of Islands the fishing industry has been successfully carried on for many years. Harbour facilities have greatly improved since the entry of Newfoundland into confederation. I am sure they will continue to be improved for the benefit of those who seek to take their living from the sea.
Here at the mouth of the Humber river and 30 miles inland from the gulf of St. Lawrence is the modern town of Corner Brook, site of the great Bowater's pulp and paper mill. It is the largest integrated newsprint mill in the world. This plant has an annual production of over 350,000 tons of newsprint and sulphite, and employs over 6,000 workers. It is an efficiently operated unit with an enviable record of relations between management and labour. One can surely appreciate the impact which this mill has had on the economy of the province since its construction in the early twenties.
While talking about the pulp and paper industry in my riding it might be well for us to have a look at this industry throughout Canada as a whole. It has been the leading industry in Canada for many years. In value of production, in exports, in total wages paid and in capital investment it is the largest of all Canadian industries. It is Canada's largest consumer of goods and services, including transportation. The newsprint industry in Canada has five times the output of the industry in any other country, and supplies one-half the world's newsprint needs. The expansion of this industry must naturally take into account the fact that raw material is the prime factor.
The Address-Mr. Batten
Canada's forests, totalling nearly 1 [DOT] 5 million square miles, are amongst the largest in the world, with over 800,000 square miles capable of producing continuous wood crops. In this house we have been hearing a great deal in the last few days about the reduction in exports and loss of foreign markets. Such is not the case so far as this industry is concerned. Shipments from Canadian mills in October last set a new record, which was again broken in November. Shipments in November, 1954, showed an increase of 10-5 per cent over shipments for the corresponding month in 1953. Newsprint Data, 1954 edition, published by the newsprint association of Canada, states that Canada is rapidly regaining its overseas markets and estimates that shipments to the United Kingdom in 1955 will very nearly equal the pre-war level.
Coming back to a description of my riding, the area extending north from the bay of Islands along the west coast of the northern peninsula, toward Labrador, is known as St. Barbe. For many decades the men along this coast have fought to earn a living from the sea. In many places wharves and breakwaters have been built, but much still remains to be done if those who live in the area are to be enabled to earn their living from the sea. Logging and lumbering offer employment as a supplement to fishing. Here again, from the scenic Bonne bay to the wave-lashed shores of the strait of Belle Isle, are long stretches of straight coast line with very few harbours, inhabited by people whose resolute sturdiness is excelled only by their hospitality.
From the early days of its discovery Newfoundland has been recognized as a fishing country. For many years it flourished as a result of the great demand of the European and South American markets for fish. During the 1920's large quantities of Newfoundland cod were sold to Spain, Portugal and Brazil. Following this period the markets open to us were gradually closed. Spain and Portugal expanded their own fishing industries to the point where the demand was considerably reduced. Methods of fishing other than those normally used produced a quantity of small fish not acceptable in some markets, particularly those of Portugal. Then there were the difficulties presented by countries willing to barter, as well as those presented by countries in the sterling area. Added to all this was the difference in standards of living, which resulted in the seller's minimum price sometimes being higher than the buyer's maximum price.
In Canada the fishing industry is one of the country's oldest, but over the years it has lost some of its relative importance. In the
702	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Batten coastal regions it is still of paramount importance, a fact which is particularly true of Newfoundland. Today 19,000 fishermen in 1,000 small hamlets scattered over 10,000 miles of coast line strive to eke a living from the sea. It has been done successfully in the past, and I believe it can be done again through the introduction of better methods of catching, curing and marketing a quality product. Figures for 1946 to 1952 show that the maritime provinces have pretty well maintained their share of the national total, and while comparable figures for Newfoundland are not available I believe the same statement is virtually true.
For those who would build dungeons in the air I would point out that the Canadian fishing industry, too, had a favourable year in 1954. For the first ten months of 1954 the catch was 11 per cent higher in volume and 8 per cent higher in value than for a similar period in 1953. Larger sales of fillets to the United States and of canned salmon to the United Kingdom resulted in a 12 per cent increase in export value over the previous year. In Newfoundland there were indications of the result of negotiations carried on last year by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) in an effort to reopen European markets which were formerly big buyers of Newfoundland products.
The fishing industry in Newfoundland has always been, and very likely must continue to be, very dependent upon foreign trade. Newfoundland, along with the other maritime provinces and the prairie provinces, must be deeply concerned with any trade policy this government may adopt. Certainly a policy of protective tariffs would not be conducive to the best trading possibilities at a time when, due to conditions over many of which we have no control, we are already having difficulty in competing in foreign markets.
Here in Canada we are in quite a different position with regard to export trade than is the United Kingdom or the United States. England, with its relatively large population and consequent large domestic market, has an export trade of 17 per cent of its total trade. Similarly in the United States, where a tremendous interstate trade is carried on, only 6 per cent of its total trade is on an international level. Here in Canada we have a relatively small population with a proportionately high degree of production, and an export trade of approximately 25 per cent of our total trade.
The future of this country depends upon the high volume of our export trade. Our economic future is dependent upon our strong competitive position in world markets. I believe that to hide behind higher tariff


barriers at this time would be to mortgage that future. In my opinion this policy is the correct one for Canada in general to follow. Certainly it is the correct policy that will breathe life into the fisheries of Newfoundland.
Many improvements have been made there, and I am sure others will come. But in the final analysis success will depend upon being able to sell our products at prices which will give a living wage to 19,000 fishermen whose homes now dot the shores of an island that was recognized as a great fishing province when the wind was still blowing through the forests on the sites of every major industry on the Canadian mainland. But I do believe that for the industry to be attractive it must not only offer opportunity for making a living, but must also be able to offer some of the benefits now granted to workers in other occupations.
In the speech from the throne we were informed that the government proposed this session to introduce legislation granting loans to fishermen' similar to those granted to farmers under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. This, I believe, is a step in the right direction, and I commend the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) for his action in this regard.
During the last session of parliament, and again early in this session, there has been mention of unemployment insurance for fishermen. Although I am not unmindful of the many difficulties to be overcome before such benefits could be extended, I believe it is possible, and would give my support to such a measure. In commercial fish establishments those who are engaged are eligible for unemployment insurance, yet the initial producer who makes these jobs possible is denied this benefit.
In my constituency there are many fishermen who, in order to earn a living for their families, are forced to supplement their low incomes from the fishing industry by work in the woods when employment is available, during part of the winter months. Many of these do not qualify for insurance benefits. If, however, by some formula they could be given credit for summer work, then they would be eligible for benefits during the winter months. I would join with my other colleagues from Newfoundland who have made reference to this matter in recommending to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) that consideration be given to such a measure.
Now, while discussing the fisheries of Newfoundland there are two other points I should like to mention. In my riding

within the last tew years, the lobster industry has assumed such proportions as to become of major concern to the fishermen in the area. Lobsters are caught in the conventional lobster traps, held in pools and shipped to the United States markets by boat. Fishermen who during the past summer prosecuted this type of fishing had a better than average year, so far as the quantity caught was concerned, but did not receive proportionate returns due to the fact that a large percentage of the catch was unsuitable upon arrival at the market. Too large a percentage was either dead, weak or maimed.
I have no figures which would suggest the average loss, but I did see individual accounts showing, in extreme cases, a loss of over 20 per cent. Whether these losses are due to improper care during the preshipment period or due to faulty methods of shipping is difficult to determine. But it is a problem which is causing some concern, and is one that needs some attention, not only from the standpoint of the return to the fishermen but also in the interests of conservation. In 1953 the federal Department of Fisheries completed experiments on the commercial holding of live lobsters. I believe these experiments are important to this industry in avoiding the causes of mortality among lobsters during the pre-shipment period.
The province of Newfoundland will not only be known as a great centre for commercial fishing, but also for sport fishing at its very best. In my riding are some of the finest trout streams and salmon pools on the North American continent. Here is a sportsman's paradise that even the expert on fish stories need not hesitate to describe. We in Newfoundland believe that this is our greatest tourist attraction, and it is our hope that with the new ferry on the gulf of St. Lawrence and the completion of the trans-Canada highway, visitors and sportsmen will be encouraged to come to our province during the summer months. In this instance there is little need for me to emphasize the importance of conservation methods. On some rivers the federal Department of Fisheries has conducted experiments, and on others improvements have been made. May I suggest a continuance of this program.
I believe that Canadians have a very healthy respect for conservation. In a land so bountifully blessed with natural resources it augurs well for the future that some thought is given to posterity's welfare. But our thoughts for tomorrow must sometimes be expressed in regulations to ensure that conservation is not only a mental attitude but also a practical reality. In the case of which
The Address-Mr. Batten I am speaking-the salmon rivers-I trust that present regulations will be enforced by river guardians and others who are concerned with such matters, and that other regulations will be designed if necessary so that this resource, which I say again is our greatest tourist attraction, will not only continue to bring visitors to our province but will also continue to afford to Newfoundlanders the joy of "fishing on a river on a morn in mid-July".
The Disabled Persons Act passed by this parliament last session and proclaimed on January 1 of this year has already received wide approval. I feel it will be welcomed as a needed addition to our present social security program, when it comes into effect in the different provinces. In my own province of Newfoundland this allowance for totally and permanently disabled persons will go into effect on April 1 of this year.
I was pleased to note in the speech from the throne that amendments are to be made during this session of parliament to the Blind Persons Act of 1952. It will be remembered that by that act the basic pension had been doubled, the residence requirements reduced by one-half, the income ceiling approximately doubled and the minimum age reduced to 21 years. It is now proposed to lower still farther the age of eligibility and to raise the income ceiling.
I am sure these amendments are understandable and welcome. While only a small number of Newfoundlanders will be affected, yet the percentage involved will be the third highest of all the provinces and nearly double the average for the whole of Canada. For the year ending March 31, 1954 the report of the department of welfare of Newfoundland records 335 persons as recipients of blind persons' allowances, which is 0-183 per cent of the population from age 20 to 69 years and 0 086 per cent of the total population of the province.
Here again is evidence of the ever-expanding social services of this nation to include within its scope not only the majority groups but also the smaller minority groups that form a part of the population of this land.
During this session of parliament amendments are to be made to the War Veterans Allowance Act. The proposed improvements to increase the basic allowance and raise the income ceiling will not only prove to be very acceptable to the 42,000 veterans and widows of veterans at present benefiting under the existing act, but will also be recognized by the citizens of Canada as another worthy advance in a program already recognized for its distinction.
704	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Perron Now, Mr. Speaker, we do have our problems in my riding, as they do in the other ridings in Newfoundland and in the other 258 ridings on the mainland of Canada. Some of these are problems of recent origin. Others are problems that have been handed down to us by a very severe history. We have those problems discussed sometimes by one group and sometimes by another. Sometimes we have people who spend an hour or two in the province, or in my riding, and without any knowledge of the historical background or of the local setting proceed to pronounce what the policies ought to be. I fear, Mr. Speaker, that I shall have to classify those people as itinerant victims of a midsummer night's dream. But we do have our problems, sir, and on the most important we usually reach solutions that are fairly satisfactory, even though sometimes the majority be small.
It has been said in this house that the fortunes of Newfoundland are at a very low ebb. With that statement, Mr. Speaker, I would have to very sincerely disagree. If we were to compare the lot of Newfoundlanders 20 years ago with the lot of Newfoundlanders now we would find a tremendous difference; and even if we were to take that 20-year period and divide it into four five-year periods, we would find that there is not only a difference between now and 20 years ago but there has been a successive improvement over those four five-year periods. We have today in Newfoundland, for example, a standard of living that may not be as high as in some places on the mainland, but that is immeasurably higher than it was 20 years ago. The year 1953 was a good year for Newfoundland; 1954 was not so good, but still a good year. Even at this present moment, for example, the unemployment situation in Newfoundland is better than it was at this time last year.
No, Mr. Speaker; the fortunes of Newfoundland are not at a low ebb, for I believe that the fortunes of any people are not manifested only in the material things which they bless and which they are blessed by. The fortunes of a people are also in the things for which they have some respect, in the things in which they have faith. We as new Canadians come to this mainland of Canada and bring with us a respect for the institution of Canadian democracy, a faith in the future of this great land, that if excelled at all will be excelled only by those who have always had the privilege of calling themselves Canadians.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, several members having congratulated the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder 

(Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, which is quite in order and well deserved by the members in question, have proceeded to criticize the speech from the throne for several reasons. As far as I am concerned, since it is not up to me to eulogize it, I would like to say a few words on a matter of interest to the economy of this country as a whole. This question has been raised several times since the beginning of this debate, though no mention has been made of it in the speech from the throne, a fact which is somewhat surprising. I refer to the question of agriculture, which is certainly the most important at this time, in the west as well as in the east. Since I have been here, I have heard it said repeatedly that the western farmer is not in an excellent position, and that he even has wheat surpluses of which he cannot dispose. On the other hand our eastern farmers complain that their revenue has considerably diminished this year again and that they view the future with some misgivings.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, if this be not a serious depression it is something rather similar; we are moving in that direction. In order to satisfy everyone I could say that our farmers are at present in the midst of a disturbance which the government claim to be temporary but which shows signs of going on indefinitely.
Still, if we read the speech from the throne all we see there with regard to agriculture and to the urgent problems which the government have to solve is this. I am quoting from page 3 of Hansard,:
Although the national economy is in a generally healthy condition, the relatively poor wheat crop is being reflected by a small decline in the total national income.
Mr. Speaker, that is absolutely all there is in the speech from the throne to solve what the government call a disturbance, but what you and I would call a depression. There is no clear remedy proposed.
And moreover, this single sentence from the speech from the throne which hardly touches upon the problem at all, bears no relation whatever to the facts. It is simply not true that the relatively poor wheat crop has brought about a slight decrease in national revenue, since this crop has not yet been sold. We still have to sell enormous surplus stocks of wheat before marketing the 1954 crop. Whether that crop has been good or bad can in no way bear upon the national revenue for 1954.
What might have had an adverse effect on this revenue-a fact which is not mentioned in the speech from the throne-is that the eastern farmer, besides having had a

poor crop, has sold his products at lower prices, failing a proper market, so that his personal revenue has decreased as much as 15 per cent, and much more than that in certain areas.
There is unquestionably an urgent problem to solve, and the fact that the speech from the throne makes no mention at all of the steps the government intends to take to help the farmer is not easy to explain.
There is no hiding the fact, farmers are concerned and expect from this government the assistance required by the situation. The only stable income they have been able to rely on for the past few years has been the income from the dairy industry, thanks to the support price of 58 cents a pound for butter.
However, the government have not yet announced the policy they intend to adopt in this connection this year, which keeps the farmers in a state of concern.
It appears to me necessary that the government maintain the price support at the same level.
This price of 58 cents was set in April, 1951 and I think it can safely be said that, since that date, production costs have increased. However, the price has remained the same. The only reason which would justify a reduction of the support price would be a reduction in the production costs. According to estimates, production costs this year will remain the same as in 1954. Such, at least, are the conclusions reached by experts of the Department of Agriculture in the course of a recent federal-provincial agricultural conference.
As another argument, I must say that, from March 1949, when it was put into effect, to January 1, 1955, price support will have cost the taxpayer, if I am rightly informed, less than $2 million, that is to say an average of about $300,000 a year. It involves a relatively minor expense to ensure a bit of security to a class of society which is the most important in the country and whose other sources of income at the present time, barring the dairy industry, are influenced by all sorts of risks, making them uncertain and precarious.
The poor crop of last year, due to bad weather, not only caused farmers to lose some income, but, in 1955, they will be faced with a shortage of seed which will entail the additional expense of a few hundred dollars for each one of them, come sowing time. Serious difficulties are anticipated, at least in the province of Quebec, next spring, to the extent that the government may have to help by means of subsidies. Were the sup-nort price of butter to be abolished, at a 50433-45
The Address-Mr. Deschatelets time when farmers will be faced by these extraordinary expenses, that would no doubt spell disaster.
In order to face the seasonal unemployment crisis, the house recently amended the Unemployment Insurance Act with a view to increasing unemployment insurance benefits. This was a humanitarian measure that the house approved unanimously. However, this measure will involve considerable outlays and it seems to me that the government should not be stingy when it comes to helping the farmer who, also, is entitled to a minimum of security.
As far as the consumer is concerned, I do not think that he is affected by the support price. Because of the support price the consumer always pays the same price for his butter, whereas he would pay, let us say, 45 cents during the production season, when there is plenty of butter, that is during the summer months, but during the off season, that is in the winter months, he would pay 75 cents, which in terms of money paid out amounts to exactly the same thing, that is 60 cents the year round. Therefore the support price has the merit of saving that commodity from the ups and downs of a market which can easily be made to fluctuate.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I ask the government to maintain the 58 cents a pound support price and to announce such a policy as soon as possible so as to put an end to the uncertainty now prevailing. The price should be set at 58 cents for the next two years as called for by all farm organizations throughout the country.
By so doing the government will assure a minimum revenue to every farmer in eastern Canada where farming is the principal industry.
If it were announced immediately, such a policy would make up for the silence kept on that score in the speech from the throne.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I represent in this house a county with a mostly working class population, and I would briefly like to comment on certain legislation mentioned in the speech from the throne that bears upon employment.
It would be well to consider first the degree of economic activity in the past year, in order to comfort our friends in the opposition, for, in spite of their claims, the general position is a good one, and I have always thought that official statistics give better information than speculations and near-truths.
The gross national product for 1954 amounts to $23 -9 billion whereas it attained $24-3 billion in 1953, or a mere 2 per cent variation, which shows an appreciable stability in our production.

The Address-Mr. Deschatelets
Consumer purchases reached a higher total in 1954 than in 1953, a fact denoting a still very high level of national purchasing power.
At the end of October industrial production in general shows only an average 2 per cent recession with regard to the year before. It should be noted, however, that the total amount for October, 1954 is higher than the corresponding figure in 1953.
And, if it is otherwise true that employment in the manufacturing industries is slightly down, employees in those industries have, on the other hand, had an hourly wage increase of 3 cents an hour in 1954.
These various glimpses of our economy therefore illustrate that business in Canada is, on the whole, good; if there have been recessions in some sectors they have been compensated elsewhere by a fuller activity.
Yet I have to admit that as far as employment is concerned, the position is still difficult, and I shall try to discuss it as objectively as possible. I do not want unduly to minimize certain figures mentioned by opposition members with regard to the number of unemployed in this country, but we must admit that statistics in this respect are incomplete and do not always give a true picture of the facts.
But, whatever might be the correct number of unemployed and the nature of that unemployment, whether it be seasonal, local or otherwise, the number of unemployed is large enough to warrant the government to take without delay important legislative measures, because private industry is now unable to absorb the unemployed.
These measures, as forecast in the speech from the throne, will no doubt give to the industry the necessary priming. I would like to say a few words about some of those measures.
Public works are required to supplement private enterprise and provide here and there urgent improvements. We have to remember that the purpose of taxation is to provide services, and it is to be hoped that those public works will be soon under way. I would like here, in passing, to suggest to the government to take into consideration the building of a new bridge on the St. Lawrence river at the end of Pie IX boulevard; when I am suggesting the building of this additional bridge for Montreal, what I have in mind is the speeding up of traffic. As a matter of fact, all the traffic coming from the eastern part of the city must now go through the centre part of the town in order to cross Jacques Cartier bridge; this Pie IX boulevard bridge would link the south shore of the river with eastern Montreal, and
TMr. Deschatelets.]

would connect directly the Laurentian highway with Pie IX boulevard at St. Vincent de Paul.
But the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterways will bring about a situation which will make the building of that Pie IX bridge still more urgent. Experts of the Montreal town planning committee anticipate that, as a result of the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway, Montreal will cease to be an island town, and the south shore municipalities will lose their rural characteristics and become industrial and residential districts. We must, therefore, increase the number of bridges spanning the St. Lawrence river, and I believe that the present conditions warrant the government to build a bridge at the Pie IX boulevard without delay.
The amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act was urgently required. The duration and rate of supplementary winter benefits are increased from now on, and the working people are now in a position to appreciate fully the wisdom of that legislation; approximately 80 per cent of salaried people are eligible for unemployment insurance benefits, and, in case of unemployment, municipalities will not have, as before, to feel the main impact of unemployment.
This amendment to the act will be beneficial, but it will be necessary to keep a close watch on the development of our national economy in order to bring down new amendments if conditions should make it necessary, and the future will prove no doubt that this beneficial act will remain among the major achievements of the Liberal party.
May I repeat the request I made last year to the government for the opening of an unemployment insurance and employment office in the east end of Montreal in order to accommodate the workers in that part of the city.
The west, north and south ends of the city of Montreal are well served at the present time, but I do not think that the Delorimier street office in Montreal is very convenient for our workers who live in the east end of the city. Moreover the eastern part of Montreal is surrounded by small industries and the opening of such an office there would be well justified. I repeat this request and hope that it will be acted upon this very year, thus sparing me the obligation of renewing my request.
Another piece of legislation forecast in the speech from the throne and which will help relieve unemployment has to do with loans for home improvements. The National Housing Act has brought results in line with the

government's expectations, in spite of the pessimistic predictions expressed at that time by the opposition. With this important improvement, it is logical to foresee a new high for 1955.
The riding of Maisonneuve-Rosemont is perhaps among those which benefited the most from that legislation. From the projects for 1955, we can anticipate a substantial increase in house building which will turn that part of the city into one of the finest residential districts. It must be admitted that in enacting this act the government has been equal to its responsibilities and, on behalf of the thousands of new home owners of my riding who have taken advantage of that legislation, I do want to thank the government.
The speech from the throne mentions also the meeting of the commonwealth prime ministers, which is now taking place in order to discuss certain common problems which are facing the peoples of that great association of nations. This conference is being held at a particularly important moment, and it will no doubt favour an exchange of views that might lead to an increase of our exports, even though it is not the immediate purpose of this meeting.
Our foreign trade is closely related to the prosperity of the Canadian people, and all efforts must be directed to the finding of new markets. But, let us be realistic, and the views expressed by the right hon. Prime Minister on January 10, 1955, are shared by the majority of Canadians. International trade must work in both directions, and, at a time when the most important nations are trying to find the way to facilitate trade, it would be suicidal to raise tariff barriers as some members of the opposition seem to want.
It is the duty of the government to organize production and to find markets. But Canadian industry also has its responsibilities, and it is up to industry to revise its means of production, in order to be able to compete with foreign goods, insofar as originality, quality and price are concerned.
I believe that the present employment difficulties in certain fields stem mainly from the lew methods of industrial adjustment and from the necessity for employers to lower their cost of production by saving on manpower.
I am satisfied that the unemployment situation is but temporary. Although the government is determined to find a solution to the iroblem, we must be grateful that it acts 50433-45i
The Address-Mr. Deschatelets cautiously, because the economy of a country is not like an automobile which can be stopped or put in motion at will. Canadian electors have shown that they understand this because at the recent by-elections they have again supported us.
Now I would like to speak about seasonal unemployment. Owing to the weather conditions in our country, we experience a shrinkage in employment every year as soon as winter sets in, but the situation improves slowly until spring.
It is not easy to find a solution to that problem. Members of the house who know the working people, who live with them, know very well that our painters, carpenters, masons, bricklayers, diggers and day-labourers may be without work for a few months each year; it is an unfortunate situation to which we should strive to find a solution. Moreover, the problem becomes more acute because several industries tend to lay off some of their employees in November and December and then hire them back towards the end of January each year.
I have studied the situation and discussed it with several workers. I believe that the practical solution rests more with the public than with the government; the time has come when everyone should realize that the government is not the only one which has a responsibility in the matter, but that it is the responsibility of the nation as a whole.
I am satisfied that, at the very moment I am speaking, work could be found in Canada for more than 100,000 unemployed if everyone assumed his share of responsibility for the solution of the problem.
It is a matter of co-ordinating the well known sense of citizenship and co-operation of all Canadians and it is in that spirit that I would like to offer a suggestion to alleviate seasonal unemployment which afflicts us and I offer it for study to both employers and organized labour.
I would like to see the setting up of an agency which would undertake, each year in January, a national eight-day employment campaign across Canada. It would surely be patronized by the Department of Labour and in all provinces, either through the press, radio or television, an appeal could be made to the public, asking everyone's co-operation to promote employment during that season.
A campaign such as this would undoubtedly receive the support of all the provincial governments as well as the wholehearted

The Address-Mr. Deschatelets support of all municipalities, and there are more than 14,000 in Canada. Since they are directly interested in promoting employment in their locality, in all those centres a proclamation by the mayor would invite all citizens to co-operate in the campaign, which would be everybody's business, as everyone would benefit from it.
We have in the country a tremendous commercial and industrial potential of over 100,000 industries of all kinds. If such a national movement were well organized, how many industries, manufactures, plants or businesses of all kinds, how many citizens, who are postponing various kinds of undertaking, even in their home, could not then become employers of labour?
And we have the necessary set-up to serve as intermediary between demand and supply, because our employment offices are scattered all over the country. The requests for labour coming from industries, business firms and private citizens would be filled by our employment offices and workers would be called to work, each according to his own skill.
Many agencies organize each year public drives to collect millions of dollars for deserving causes and their campaigns are always most successful. Why not then invite the cooperation of all Canadians to such a national employment campaign, which would no doubt be as important as all the other ones? A national employment campaign is a suggestion I make and possibly it deserves consideration.
I should now like to comment on the deplorable situation created for workers who are being rushed into retirement when they reach 65. Since I became a member of the house, I have very often had the opportunity to discuss with them and to appraise the extent of the injustice of which they are very often the victims.
Our society entertains a prejudice concerning the worker of 65 years of age, and I have noted in the papers that the British ministry of pensions carried out a survey in this matter. I believe the lessons taught by this survey would apply here as well as elsewhere.
As it appears from that survey, the majority of workers who took their pension at the age of 65, were compelled to do so at a moment when their employers were still benefiting from their energy, their good will and, especially, their experience. At that age, no doubt, physical strength wanes but any deficiency in that respect is largely offset by Knowledge and experience. We are here the

victims of a preconceived idea. As a matter of fact, some men are already old at 40, while others are still young at 65.
Would it not be possible for us to take the leadership, as far as our own civil servants are concerned, and set an example for industry to follow? And if such a survey were made here, the perpetration of a great many injustices might well be prevented.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I regret to be under the obligation to comment on certain remarks made in this house, January 12, by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier). These remarks were strongly objected to by members from Quebec sitting on either side of this house. I feel compelled also to object in like manner to the statement made by that hon. member, as reported at page 121 of Hansard:
...there is no part of Canada that is as ripe for advances by the communist party as the province of Quebec.
Travel broadens, we are told, and it is to be hoped that this hon. member, a new incarnation of the political commercial traveller, will take the first opportunity to return to the province of Quebec so that he might get to know it as it really is, a province securely rooted in traditions of religion, culture and hospitality and, above all, respectful of authority.
On January 17 he made an attempt to clarify his speech of January 12, stating that he had . . .
. . . the greatest regard for the religion, language, heritage and culture of the people of that province.
This clarification bears no relation, however, with the astounding statement he made on January 12, to the effect that no part of Canada was so ripe for advances by the communist party as the province of Quebec.
And that is why, on behalf of the 50,000 constituents of Maisonneuve-Rosemont whom I have the honour to represent, I indict this statement as false and I dare hope that the leader of his group will dissociate himself from this false and humiliating statement about the province of Quebec.
Since then, other unfavourable remarks have been made by members of the C.C.F. party against the province of Quebec. Nothing could be more harmful to national unity than such remarks which only serve to stir animosity and mistrust.
Last year, I asked what good purpose was served by all these speeches on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Experience shows me now that the Canadian electorate can derive benefit from such speeches because they help remove a good number of masks and, most of all, they prove

The Address-Mr. Weselak
to the electorate that they were right in showing confidence in the Liberal party which traditionally has respected the rights of minorities in Canada and treated all groups and all provinces with fair play, not for the purpose of fostering their policies but for laying the foundations of a united and prosperous nation.
